title: Book Sixteen opens: after cleansing, spiritual offerings
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK SIXTEEN. That we must bring to God spiritual sacrifices and gifts.

Cyril: What has been said is enough, I think, to show that we must go resolutely to have our sin rubbed away, and to the cleansing that comes through Christ. He is able to scour away all the filth that is in us, melting it down by the working of the Spirit, and he knows how to make us washed clean and holy. This is why the sacred word speaks to us in just this way, crying out long beforehand about the working of the Spirit that was to come upon us: ‘For suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the messenger of the covenant whom you desire. Behold, he is coming, says the Lord Almighty. And who will endure the day when he comes in? Or who will stand when he appears? For he comes in like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap, and he will sit refining and purifying, as silver and as gold.’ (Malachi 3:1–3) And in harmony with these words, too, is the inspired…
translator_notes: PG 68.1009. Heading and argument line, then Cyril's opening turn; the column cut falls after ὁ θεσπέσιος and the name Ἡσαΐας opens §2, so §1 ends with an ellipsis. γεννικῶς read as γενναίως ('resolutely', 'nobly'). The genitive participles οἵου τε … συντήκοντος … εἰδότος all agree with Χριστοῦ, so Christ is the one who scours, melts and makes holy, by the Spirit's working. Malachi 3:1–3 is LXX (πόα πλυνόντων, 'washers' herb', given as 'fullers' soap'; καθιεῖται taken as 'he will sit', as in the Hebrew). The Greek has no speaker label at the start of the book; Cyril is speaking, as in Book 15.

title: Cleansing is not enough: the Sabbath rest and the priests' sacred work
english: Cyril: …Isaiah, who says: ‘The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.’ (Isaiah 4:4) So then, Palladius, would we fully carry out the way of the righteousness understood in Christ simply by being scoured clean and by rubbing away our old defilements? Tell me, would that be enough for the glory that befits the saints, and would it crown us with the highest honors? Or rather, will our condition in some way be better, and shall we rightly adorn our own heads with the highest praise, when we bring to God, as a kind of spiritual gift and a truly sacred offering, the life lived in sanctification and holiness, and carry out spiritual worship thoroughly?
Palladius: That is what I say.

Cyril: Indeed this agrees with the sacred laws, is pleasing to God, and is among the things most approved. He commanded rest from all work on the Sabbath, and allowed no one to do anything at all, saying this in Exodus: ‘Remember the day of the Sabbath, to keep it holy. Six days you shall work and do all your works; but the seventh day is the Sabbath, a rest to the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it.’ (Exodus 20:8–10) The type plainly points to the Sabbath rest kept in spirit, when through Christ himself we have been called to cease and rest from every work of the flesh and from wicked pursuits, shaking off the burden of sin, loving to turn away from wickedness and to rest from whatever lies outside the law. For such a Sabbath rest remained out of reach for those of Israel; for they never entered Christ’s rest at all, as blessed Paul says (Hebrews 4:6–9). But Christ has given us rest, and has persuaded us to keep the Sabbath in a spiritual way, giving ourselves freely to virtue and practicing a good idleness from offenses.
Palladius: You have spoken excellently.

Cyril: Now God did indeed lay down long ago that all must rest from work on the Sabbath. Yet those crowned with the divine ministry and appointed to wait on the holy tent still performed the sacred rites; and though they profaned the Sabbath, as the Savior says, they were blameless (Matthew 12:5), and did not face the charge of having broken the law. So we too, in Christ, shall cease from earthly pursuits, fulfilling the inward Sabbath rest; but we shall not hold back from the sacred works — I mean, from our duty to bring God spiritual sacrifices and inward gifts (1 Peter 2:5). Following, as it is written, in the footsteps of Christ (1 Peter 2:21), we shall offer ourselves in sacrifice, honoring the God of all not with slaughtered sheep and the blood of calves, but rather dedicating ourselves to him as a fragrant aroma. For we shall please him more than a young calf that puts forth horns and hoofs, as the Psalmist says (Psalm 69:31).
Palladius: You think rightly. But come now, go on once more: from the…
translator_notes: PG 68.1012. Continues Cyril's sentence from §1. Οὕτω φημί ('So I say') is Palladius agreeing with Cyril's second alternative (that we must also offer a holy life), not with the first. The subject of προστέταχεν and ἠφίει is unexpressed; the masculine λέγων and the preceding Θεῷ κεχαρισμένον point to God, so the English gives 'He'. Ἀπελείπετο … τοῖς ἐξ Ἰσραήλ echoes Hebrews 4:9 (ἀπολείπεται σαββατισμός): rendered 'remained out of reach for those of Israel' to keep Cyril's point that Israel never reached it; Cyril attributes Hebrews to Paul and speaks of 'Christ's rest' where Hebrews says 'His [God's] rest'. Ἡμᾶς δὲ κατέπαυσεν ὁ Χριστός plays on Hebrews 4:8 (εἰ αὐτοὺς Ἰησοῦς κατέπαυσεν), covered by the same citation. Γραφή here is a legal indictment, hence 'face the charge'. Νοητός/νοητῶς (spiritual, perceived by the mind) rendered 'inward' or 'in a spiritual way' to keep it distinct from πνευματικός ('spiritual'). 'Spiritual sacrifices' (θυσίας πνευματικάς) cited to 1 Peter 2:5, the only New Testament source of the phrase; 'following in the footsteps' (ἴχνεσι, κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον) to 1 Peter 2:21. Psalm 68:32 LXX = Psalm 69:31 in English Bibles. Εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας is stock sacrificial language (Leviticus passim; compare Ephesians 5:2); left uncited as doubtful. The column cut falls inside Palladius's sentence (καὶ ἐξ / ἱερῶν Γραμμάτων).

title: The whole burnt offering: each gives his whole life as he is able
english: Palladius: …sacred Scriptures, sketch out the outlines of this splendid and admirable worship.

Cyril: Well then, God said in Leviticus, and plainly to all those of Israel: ‘If any one of you brings gifts to the Lord, you shall bring your gifts from the livestock, from the cattle and from the sheep. If his gift is a whole burnt offering from the cattle, he shall bring a male without blemish; he shall bring it to the door of the tent of witness, acceptable before the Lord. And he shall lay his hand on the head of the offering, acceptable for him, to make atonement for him. And he shall slaughter the calf before the Lord, and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall bring the blood and pour the blood on the altar all around, the altar that is at the doors of the tent of witness. And when they have flayed the whole burnt offering, they shall cut it up limb by limb; and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall put fire on the altar and pile wood on the fire; and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall lay the cut pieces, the head and the fat on the wood that is on the fire upon the altar; but the entrails and the feet they shall wash with water, and the priest shall lay all of it on the altar. It is an offering, a sacrifice, a fragrant aroma to the Lord.’ (Leviticus 1:2–9) Is this not a clear type of the life of the saints, and of their complete closeness to God in spirit and sanctification? For we are pictured in the tame animals — the calf, I mean, and the sheep — dying to the world by putting the flesh to death, so that we may live to God through the Gospel way of life, and going up, as it were, as a sacrifice that is truly spiritual and most fragrant, offered through the Son to the Father. And come, let us go through each point again for you, as finely as we can.

For each one dedicates his own life as a kind of gift to God, who rules over all, but as it is given to each, and according to the measure he has. For one has his own gift from God in one way, and another in another, as the most wise Paul says (1 Corinthians 7:7). In the sizes of the animals, that is, in their differences of kind, the inequality and unlikeness among us — in spiritual strength, perhaps, and in strength of mind — is hinted at indirectly. So whether someone happens to be great, as in the calf, and very strong indeed, or has less, as in the sheep, and falls short of perfection, he brings himself to God as a gift, and that as a whole burnt offering, that is, as an entire dedication. He does not keep his life divided toward the things of the world, but keeps it whole and entire, acceptable and holy to God.

Let the manner of the sacrifice be such as this: ‘Let the victim be male and without blemish,’ it says (Leviticus 1:3). For the saints are always in some way conformed to Christ, who is truly male and without blemish: ‘male’ describes his power to lead, and ‘without blemish’ his holiness, which is beyond nature and cannot be surpassed. For we have one Leader, pure beyond all compare: Emmanuel (Matthew 23:10). In another sense too (for this too must be said, and I judge that it must)…
translator_notes: PG 68.1013. Opens mid-sentence inside Palladius's request; ἀνατύπου is an imperative addressed to Cyril (Palladius asks him to sketch the outlines from Scripture), and γραφάς here means 'outlines, pictures' (with ἀνατύπου, 'shape out'), not 'Scriptures'. The long quotation is Leviticus 1:2–9 LXX, and the English follows Cyril's wording; in v. 9 his text has singular ὁ ἱερεύς ('the priest'), where printed LXX editions may read the plural οἱ ἱερεῖς. Κάρπωμα rendered 'offering' to keep it distinct from ὁλοκαύτωμα 'whole burnt offering'. Ἰσχνοεποῦντες ('speaking finely, in detail') given as 'as finely as we can'. 1 Corinthians 7:7 is quoted almost word for word (ἴδιον ἔχων ἐκ Θεοῦ χάρισμα, ὁ μὲν οὕτως, ὁ δὲ οὕτως). Τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, 'the ruling/leading quality', given as 'his power to lead'. Εἷς … καθηγητής follows Matthew 23:10 (εἷς γάρ ἐστιν ὑμῶν ὁ καθηγητής, ὁ Χριστός). Uncited possible echoes, left without citation as doubtful: 'die to the world … so that we may live to God' (compare Galatians 2:19; Romans 6:11); 'as it is given to each … measure' (compare Romans 12:3; Ephesians 4:7); 'not divided' (compare 1 Corinthians 7:33–34); 'acceptable and holy' (compare Romans 12:1); σύμμορφοι (compare Romans 8:29). Editorial brackets in the source: δεῖ[ν] and [καὶ] (ἱερὰν) are printed as supplied; the English follows the supplied text. The sentence beginning Ἄλλως τε runs into §4.

title: Male and without blemish: slaughter, blood and flaying as dying to the world
english: Cyril: …it would be fitting for those consecrated to God to be male and without blemish: with nothing effeminate about them, not given over to sloth, but firmly bent on showing manly courage, and keeping the mind within them manly and, as it were, wide awake. And I would add this as well: they must be pure and without blemish, at least as far as human nature allows. For somewhere the inspired David sings, and very wisely: ‘Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to my innocence that is in me.’ (Psalm 7:8) For with God the standard of human goodness is in some way measured to fit us, while that of the holy angels plainly rises higher and far exceeds our measure. So let the holy victim be male and without blemish.

It is brought to the very doors of the holy tent (Leviticus 1:3). For we are made perfect nowhere else than in the churches, since it is there, wholly and in every way, that we shall be acceptable to God the Father, with Christ as priest bringing us to him. For through him we have obtained access (Romans 5:2; Ephesians 2:18), and he himself opened for us the way in (Hebrews 10:19–20), entering the Holy of Holies as forerunner on our behalf (Hebrews 6:20), and showing us the true path. God also commanded them to lay their hands on the calf (Leviticus 1:4), hinting at this indirectly: that in place of themselves they offer, in type, an image of our need to live in holiness by dying to the world, when they duly carry out the slaughter of the beast.

See, then, how the shadow gives shape to the truth for us. The calf was slaughtered before the Lord, and the blood was poured out on the altar (Leviticus 1:5). For dying to the world, and putting to death the impulses of the flesh, is most pleasing to God and worthy of his gaze from above. And perhaps our godly David sings of something like this when he says: ‘Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones.’ (Psalm 116:15) For the death of the holy ones will be like a sacred offering to God; and surely I do not mean the death of all who live in the flesh. Rather, the word would point us to the death they are accustomed to endure, dying to the world but living to God in holiness and sanctification. For it is impossible for us to achieve the holy life unless we have first died to the world. For Peter writes about Christ: ‘He bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live to righteousness.’ (1 Peter 2:24) So the slaughter of the calf seems to signify dying to sins, and enduring the death that is precious with God, the death he is pleased to look upon. For ‘they shall slaughter the calf,’ it says, ‘before the Lord.’ (Leviticus 1:5) And the pouring of the blood on the altar would signify, I think, the dedication of one's life and the offering up of the soul to the glory of God.

The victim is flayed and cut up limb by limb (Leviticus 1:6). The flaying suggests a kind of stripping bare and uncovering of what is within us; the cutting into pieces shows very well that the word of God reaches down to joints and marrow (Hebrews 4:12).
translator_notes: PG 68.1016. Completes Cyril's sentence begun at the end of §3 (Ἄλλως τε … ἄρσενάς τε καὶ ἀμώμους πρέποι ἂν εἶναι). Θηλυπρεπές kept as 'effeminate', Cyril's own contrast with ἄρσεν 'male'; ἀνδρίζεσθαι 'play the man'. Psalm 7:9 LXX = Psalm 7:8 in English Bibles (ἀκακία 'innocence', Hebrew 'integrity'). Psalm 115:6 LXX = Psalm 116:15 in English Bibles. Ἐπιείκεια rendered 'goodness'; the point is that God measures human goodness by a human standard, below the angels'. 'Οὐχ ἑτέρωσέ ποι, ἢ ὅτι' rendered 'nowhere else than in the churches, since it is there…'. Δι' αὐτοῦ … τὴν προσαγωγὴν ἐσχήκαμεν joins Romans 5:2 (τὴν προσαγωγὴν ἐσχήκαμεν) and Ephesians 2:18 (δι' αὐτοῦ ἔχομεν τὴν προσαγωγήν); both cited. Doubtful reading: ἐνεκαίνισε τὴν εἰς τὸ εἶναι πάροδον, literally 'inaugurated the passage into being'; the Hebrews 10:19–20 context (εἴσοδον τῶν ἁγίων, ἣν ἐνεκαίνισεν ἡμῖν ὁδόν) suggests the print may stand for εἰσιέναι or εἴσω ('the way in'), so the English gives 'the way in'; the digital PG 68 text (column 1016) also prints εἰς τὸ εἶναι, so the emendation is unconfirmed and needs checking against another copy of the Greek. Πρόδρομος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν follows Hebrews 6:20. The subject of προστέταχε ('commanded') is unexpressed; given as 'God', the speaker of Leviticus in §3 (Ἔφη τοίνυν Θεὸς ἐν τῷ Λευϊτικῷ). In the hand-laying sentence, διὰ τοῦ τεθνάναι τῷ κόσμῳ is taken with βιοῦν ἁγίως ('live in holiness by dying to the world') and τὴν τοῦ κτήνους σφαγὴν εὖ μάλα ποιούμενοι as 'when they duly carry out the slaughter'; another possible reading is 'making the beast's slaughter stand for dying to the world'. Οὔτι που πάντων τῶν κατὰ σάρκα, φημί read as 'surely I do not mean the death of all who live in the flesh': the verse is not about bodily death in general; the death meant is dying to the world. Cyril's quotation of Leviticus 1:5 has plural σφάξουσι where the LXX quoted in §3 has singular σφάξει. Hebrews 4:12 is alluded to here and quoted in full at the start of §5, so it is cited at the allusion.

title: Head, entrails and feet; the lamb slain toward the north
english: Cyril: …For ‘the word of God is living,’ he says, ‘and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is hidden before him, but all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes, to whom we must give account’ (Hebrews 4:12–13). As the priest kindles the fire, the divided pieces are laid on the altar, with the head and the feet, and the entrails too, washed with water (Leviticus 1:7–9). For everything that belongs to the saints is fragrant, and nothing that is believed to be in them is rejected by God. The flesh would be a type of their life in the body, the coarser life, so to speak; for it is honorable and wholly pure. The head is a sign of the mind; the entrails stand for thoughts and desires; and the feet, in turn, are a subtle figure of the active life and of our walk, as it were, in deeds.
Palladius: How subtle the argument is!

Cyril: Even so, it holds the truth, though it flashes past us as if through mist and darkness; for the law is deep. ‘If his gift to the Lord,’ it says, ‘is from the flock, from the lambs or from the kids, for a whole burnt offering, he shall bring a male without blemish, and he shall lay his hand on its head, and they shall slaughter it at the side of the altar toward the north, before the Lord’ (Leviticus 1:10–11). This victim too is cut into pieces, and its entrails are washed, in the same way as the calf; and again he laid down that it must be carried up onto the altar (Leviticus 1:12–13). The meaning of the spiritual reading would be the same in this case as well. Yet there is one difference: the lamb was slaughtered at the side of the altar toward the north.
Palladius: What, then, is the meaning of this?

Cyril: Do you not know that the land of the Jews lies somewhat to the south, while the countless flocks of the nations have divided among themselves the regions toward the northern sea, settled in countries and cities?
Palladius: True.

Cyril: The sacrifice of the lamb in the more northern part, as it were, is therefore a figure showing that the flocks toward the north will also be holy to God. This is what the Savior too foretold about the flock from the nations, when he said: ‘And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and there will be one flock, one shepherd’ (John 10:16).
Palladius: I understand what you mean.

Cyril: The God of all sets those who choose to fulfill what the law prescribes above sloth and beyond all reluctance: he in a way smooths the road of offering, and directs that the sacrifice be completed even with creatures smaller than a sheep, saying: ‘If he brings a gift to the Lord, a burnt offering from the birds, he shall bring his gift from the turtledoves or from the doves; and the priest shall bring it to the altar, and wring off its head, and the priest shall put it on the altar, and drain its blood at the base of the altar (Leviticus 1:14–15).
translator_notes: Boundary in: section 5 opens inside Cyril’s turn; section 4 ends with the claim that the cutting into pieces shows God’s word reaching ‘joints and marrow’, so the Hebrews quotation is introduced by γάρ (‘For’) and the section starts ‘Cyril: …For’. Boundary out: the quotation of Leviticus 1:14–17 is split; the source section ends with the single word Καὶ, which opens Leviticus 1:16 (‘and he shall remove the crop’). That ‘and’ is rendered at the start of section 6, not here, so section 5 ends at ‘base of the altar (Leviticus 1:14–15).’ The opening quotation mark of the Leviticus quotation is closed in section 6. Hebrews 4:13 πρὸς ὃν ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος rendered ‘to whom we must give account’ (could also be ‘with whom we have to do’). Leviticus 1:7–9 is a paraphrase, not a quotation (LXX: the sons of Aaron put fire on the altar, lay the pieces, head and fat, wash the entrails and feet). Leviticus 1:10–11 follows the LXX, which adds ‘and he shall lay his hand on its head’ in v. 10 (not in the Hebrew of v. 10). Leviticus 1:12–13 is paraphrase (cut into pieces, wash entrails, carry all to the altar). Palladius’ Ὡς δριμὺς ὁ λόγος: δριμύς means sharp or keen; Cyril’s reply (‘it flashes past us as if through mist’) shows Palladius means the reading is subtle and hard to grasp, so ‘How subtle the argument is!’. θεωρία rendered ‘spiritual reading’ (Cyril’s term for the figurative sense). ἀγέλαι (herds) rendered ‘flocks’ to keep the sheep image that leads into John 10:16. πρὸς θάλασσαν τὴν βορειοτέραν literally ‘toward the more northern sea’; rendered ‘toward the northern sea’. LXX περιστερά in Leviticus 1:14 (English Bibles: ‘young pigeons’) is rendered ‘doves’ because section 6 reads the bird as ‘the gentlest dove’. κάρπωμα rendered ‘burnt offering’ (LXX equivalent of the whole offering here). No LXX Psalm renumbering needed in this section.

title: Turtledove and dove: Christ and the saints
english: Cyril: …and he shall remove the crop with the feathers and throw them beside the altar on the east side, into the place of the ashes; and he shall break it at the wings, but shall not divide it; and the priest shall put it on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a sacrificial burnt offering, a fragrant aroma to the Lord’ (Leviticus 1:16–17). See again how finely and skillfully their likeness to Christ has been kept for the saints. For he himself is truly the most vocal turtledove, the one from above, and likewise the gentlest dove. Indeed, in the Song of Songs it is written of him: ‘The voice of the turtledove was heard in the wilderness’ (Song of Songs 2:12). And he set himself before us as a type and pattern of the greatest and highest gentleness, saying: ‘Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart’ (Matthew 11:29). But see: because the saints themselves have come to be in the form of Christ, the beauty and the admirable worth found in goods that are, so to speak, the same have been well kept for them too. For they too may rightly be understood as turtledoves, since they send forth the divine and holy word to those who listen, and are eager to make songs and melodies for the glory of God. That is why they say: ‘My tongue shall tell of your righteousness, and of your praise all day long’ (Psalm 35:28). Moreover, they live out the life that is in Christ and hasten along the gentlest path of the Gospel way of life: to those who want to strike them on the right cheek they turn the left as well, and to those who press them into service for one mile they freely make a gift of going two, if those so choose (Matthew 5:39, 41). So they consecrate themselves to God as a fragrant aroma and as a whole burnt offering, in the form, as it were, of turtledoves and doves. Then the priest wrings off the head and puts it on the altar, having poured out the blood (Leviticus 1:15). For the mind of the holiest saints is truly holy, and holy in the highest degree, and so it would be fitting for it to be dedicated to the wholly pure God. For it is full of good thoughts, and it gives off the fragrant ointment of the true knowledge of God; for, as it is written, ‘the thoughts of the righteous are just judgments’ (Proverbs 12:5). And that the life of those who live in the fear of God is holy too would become clear from the rule that the blood must be poured out at the holy altar; for the blood is a type of life. The crop of the birds, that is, the craw, is removed together with the feathers, and it is thrown away as wholly useless. This too would be a clear sign that the life of the saints has been shown to stand above bodily indulgence, so that in a way it seems no longer to need even the stomach that holds the food. For such, in a way, is the life of those who labor most earnestly: paying no heed to food, and perhaps even to the stomach itself, they waste away the flesh and put pleasures to death, and they have become free and released from everything worldly and superfluous. This, I think, is what the casting away of the feathers means. For birds need their plumage; and we too need the things by which this body from the earth is served in its own needs: I mean clothing, and what serves for food, and besides these…
translator_notes: Boundary in: section 6 opens in the middle of the Leviticus 1:14–17 quotation begun in section 5; the closing word of section 5 (Καὶ) is rendered here as the opening ‘and’ of Leviticus 1:16. The closing quotation mark after ‘to the Lord’ answers the opening mark in section 5. Boundary out: the section ends inside a list (ἄμφια … καὶ τροφῆς ὄργανα, καὶ πρός γε δὴ τούτοις) whose last item is in section 7; English ends ‘and besides these…’. Leviticus 1:16 LXX κατ’ ἀνατολάς, ‘on the east side’. Leviticus 1:17 οὐ διελεῖ, ‘shall not divide it’ (i.e., not sever it in two). Song of Songs 2:12: Cyril reads ‘heard in the wilderness’ (ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ); the LXX reads ‘heard in our land’ (ἐν τῇ γῇ ἡμῶν). The English follows Cyril’s wording and keeps the citation, since the quotation is clear; the difference may be a slip of memory or a blend with Isaiah 40:3 (not cited). Matthew 11:29: ὅτι rendered ‘for’ (causal), as in standard English Bibles. Psalm 35:28: LXX Psalm 34:28 (exact wording: ἡ γλῶσσά μου μελετήσει τὴν δικαιοσύνην σου, ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν τὸν ἔπαινόν σου) = English Psalm 35:28. LXX Psalm 70:24 (= English 71:24) is close but its word order differs and it lacks ‘your praise’, so 35:28 is the source. Matthew 5:39, 41 is a paraphrase (right cheek / left; one mile / two); Cyril skips verse 40 (the cloak), so the citation is 5:39, 41, not 5:39–41. Proverbs 12:5 LXX λογισμοὶ δικαίων κρίματα: ‘the thoughts of the righteous are just judgments’. Uncited possible allusions: συμμορφία / ἐν μορφῇ Χριστοῦ (Romans 8:29; Galatians 4:19), ὑπογραμμός (1 Peter 2:21), songs for God’s glory (Ephesians 5:19), ‘fragrant aroma’ offering of self (Ephesians 5:2), the fragrance of the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 2:14), blood as life (Leviticus 17:11), putting pleasures to death (Colossians 3:5), the body from the earth (Genesis 2:7). The obscure phrase τὸ ἐν ἴσοις ὥσπερ ἀγαθοῖς εὐπρεπές τε καὶ ἀξιάγαστον (‘the fair and admirable [state] in equal goods, as it were’) is rendered ‘a fair and admirable share in what are, so to speak, the same goods’: the saints share Christ’s marks (turtledove, dove). στρουθία (small birds, sparrows) rendered ‘the birds’; φύσα, Cyril’s gloss on πρόλοβος, rendered ‘craw’. φιλοπονώτατοι rendered ‘those who labor most earnestly’ (ascetics). ἐκκλάσει αὐτὸ ἐκ τῶν πτερύγων rendered ‘break it at the wings’ (not ‘break it open’), because section 7 reads it as the breaking of the wings. τετήρηται (twice) kept as ‘has been kept for’ the saints; a dative of agent (‘the saints have kept’) is also possible. προσχεύσας rendered ‘having poured out the blood’ with no added ‘beside it’. πρέποι kept as a potential optative (‘would be fitting’).

title: Wings broken, body undivided; the fine flour offering
english: Cyril: …certainly also the means by which these are obtained, ways of earning money that fight off the onset of want; and soft beds, and whatever is close to these. But even if these things are useful and necessary for those who live on earth and in bodies, the saints count them as nothing. They have sent away the possession of such things as so much useless clutter, and they pass their lives in the world with bodies all but naked and unclothed, granting grudgingly to the needs of the flesh whatever comes to hand and is easily obtained. When the feathers have been plucked and the craw, that is, the crop, has been removed, ‘he shall break it,’ it says, ‘at the wings, and shall not divide it’ (Leviticus 1:17), and then he shall carry it up onto the altar. The breaking of the wings would be a type and a clear example of the mind of the saints not thinking proud thoughts, nor flying on high, but rather being drawn along with the lowly (Romans 12:16) and seeking, so to speak, the things below. For the mind of the arrogant is always lifted up somehow and carried toward the heights; it cannot bear to sit down with those of lower station, and it despises a modest and humble way of thinking. So the breaking of the wings shows in a figure the putting away of arrogance. And that it is not divided shows that they have dedicated their own life to God entirely and, if we may put it so, in every way, not divided toward the things of the world; and the wise Paul too said that those who are married are divided (1 Corinthians 7:33–34). Holy, then, is the mind of the saints, and holy their life: above bodily indulgence, free of worldly care, made beautiful by a modest mind, and undivided toward the things of the world. That is why it is dedicated to God as a fragrant aroma.
Palladius: So it is.

Cyril: He then brings the kinds of sacrifice down further, to things smaller still, things that are at hand all year round and are got without sweat, widening, I think, the road to approval for small and great alike. For it is written: ‘Your commandment is exceedingly broad’ (Psalm 119:96). With God, who loves virtue, sincerity is not judged in every case and altogether by the size of the offering; rather, the lowly person stands equal with the eminent when he gives what he has and has chosen to honor God with whatever he has and is able to give. So he spoke again in this way: ‘If a soul brings a gift, a sacrifice to the Lord, his gift shall be fine flour; and he shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it; it is a sacrifice. And he shall bring it to the sons of Aaron, the priests; and taking from it a full handful of the fine flour with the oil, and all its frankincense, the priest shall put its memorial portion on the altar; it is a sacrifice, a fragrant aroma to the Lord’ (Leviticus 2:1–2). Do you see, then, how it pointed to the lowliness of the one who brings the offering? For the divine law simply names him ‘a soul’, even if he is quite undistinguished in this life, and in this too it shows that the supreme nature is fair and impartial toward all, as indeed it does again when it says: ‘All souls are mine’ (Ezekiel 18:4). For the Godhead shows no partiality, as I said just now. So if one of those who have no distinction in the world, it says, chooses to bring a gift to God, fine flour will be the form of the sacrifice, but moistened with oil and mixed with frankincense.
translator_notes: Boundary in: section 7 opens inside the list begun in section 6 (‘I mean clothing, and what serves for food, and besides these…’); its first words εὖ μάλα καὶ τὰ δι’ ὧν ἂν γένοιτο ταυτί are rendered ‘certainly also the means by which these are obtained’ (the ‘and’ is already in section 6’s ‘and besides these…’). πορισμοὶ χρημάτων is in apposition to ‘the means’; εὐναί τε μαλακαί resumes the main list, hence the semicolon. Boundary out: the section ends with the single word ὅτι, which begins a sentence finished in section 8 (ὅτι δὲ ζωῆς μὲν εἰς τύπον ἡ σεμίδαλις … πολὺς ἡμῖν διεσάφησε λόγος, ‘That the fine flour is a type of life … we have explained at length’). ‘That’ is rendered at the start of section 8 so the reading text does not end on a dangling word. Leviticus 1:17 quoted in part (ἐκκλάσει … ἀπὸ τῶν πτερυγίων, καὶ οὐ διελεῖ); ‘carry it up onto the altar’ is Cyril’s paraphrase of the same verse. Romans 12:16 (μὴ τὰ ὑψηλὰ φρονοῦντες ἀλλὰ τοῖς ταπεινοῖς συναπαγόμενοι) is a clear verbal allusion (συνεπάγεσθαι τοῖς ταπεινοῖς), so it is cited. ‘Seeks the things below’ reverses the wording of Colossians 3:1–2 in the sense of humility; not cited. 1 Corinthians 7:33–34 (καὶ μεμέρισται): Paul says the married man is divided; Cyril generalizes to ‘those who are married’. Psalm 119:96: LXX Psalm 118:96 πλατεῖα ἡ ἐντολή σου σφόδρα = English Psalm 119:96. Leviticus 2:1–2 follows the LXX; ψυχή (‘a soul’) is kept literally because Cyril’s comment rests on that word. The participle δραξάμενος has no finite verb of its own in the LXX; rendered ‘taking from it … the priest shall put’. Ezekiel 18:4 LXX πᾶσαι αἱ ψυχαὶ ἐμαί εἰσιν. Uncited possible allusions: God shows no partiality (Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11; 1 Peter 1:17 ἀπροσωπολήμπτως); giving according to what one has (2 Corinthians 8:12; the widow’s offering, Mark 12:41–44). τὸ θεῖον rendered ‘the Godhead’ (capitalized, meaning God). ‘As I said just now’ refers to Cyril’s words two sentences earlier in this same turn (τὸ … ἶσον καὶ ἀπροκλινές, ‘fair and impartial toward all’). ὄχλος εἰκαῖος rendered ‘useless clutter’; σὺν ὄκνῳ ‘grudgingly’. ‘Is drawn along’ keeps the passive συνεπάγεσθαι. The source shows δῶ-ρον split by a line break; read as δῶρον. ἐκκλάσει rendered ‘break it’ (not ‘break it open’) to match section 6 and Cyril’s reading of the breaking of the wings. The τοῦ μὴ φρονεῖν … ζητεῖν infinitives are kept as the content of the ‘type and clear example’ (‘of the mind of the saints not thinking …’) rather than turned into a separate indicative statement.

title: Flour, oil and frankincense; God welcomes even the smallest gift
english: Cyril: …That the fine flour is a type of life, the oil a type of the cheerfulness that belongs to hope, and the frankincense a type of the fragrance that comes from good works, upright deeds and a life fully in keeping with the law, we have explained at length already. So the law says that those who choose to make the God of all rejoice in them must by all means dedicate and consecrate their own life to him, without being gloomy over the sweat that virtue costs (‘Do not grumble,’ says the inspired Paul, 1 Corinthians 10:10), a life filled full of spiritual fragrance; for then the priest will offer up its memorial portion to God (Leviticus 2:2). For we shall draw near to God the Father in Christ through spiritual sacrifice, and gain this as well: to be kept in his remembrance. By the very things through which we are used to winning approval, we shall show that we are worthy of remembrance and that we have come to be known by God in Christ.
Palladius: That was very finely said.

Cyril: To this the law adds: ‘If you bring as a gift a sacrifice baked in an oven, a gift to the Lord of fine flour: unleavened loaves kneaded with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil. If his gift is a sacrifice from the pan, it shall be fine flour kneaded with oil, unleavened; and you shall break them into pieces and pour oil on them; it is a sacrifice to the Lord. If your gift is a sacrifice from the grill, it shall be made of fine flour with oil (Leviticus 2:4–7). If you bring a sacrifice of firstfruits to the Lord, new groats, roasted and crushed, for the Lord, you shall bring the sacrifice of the firstfruits and put frankincense on them; it is a sacrifice. And the priest shall offer up its memorial portion from the groats with the oil, and all its frankincense; it is an offering to the Lord’ (Leviticus 2:14–16).
Palladius: How deep a thing the law is! Tell me, then, how we may turn our minds even to such fine details as these without straying from the mark.

Cyril: What deserves our attention here, I think, is the law’s forethought and great skill. You will certainly see it: it accepts what is very small indeed, and to that too it grants, in every case, fragrance and cheerfulness. For you have surely heard Christ himself say: ‘And whoever gives one of these brothers, the little ones, a cup of cold water to drink, only in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward’ (Matthew 10:42). We must reason in some such way here too, and applaud the Lawgiver’s kindness with the praises that befit him. For, as I said, he accepts the offering even if someone chooses to fulfill what is prescribed with the very cheapest things. For whether it is a loaf, the law says, or a single wafer, whether from the oven or from the pan or indeed from the grill, and even if it is not of wheat at all but groats and crushed grain, that is, meal made from pulse, let what is brought be moistened with oil, and let it in turn have frankincense lavished on it. And in these very details the passage seems somehow to hint to us at the approval the saints win through fiery trial and toil, and indeed through being crushed.
translator_notes: PG 68.1024. Boundary in: section 7’s English ends on ‘…mixed with frankincense.’ and leaves its last word ὅτι to this section; the whole ὅτι-clause (‘That the fine flour is a type of life … we have explained at length already’) is rendered here once. Boundary out: the last sentence (Ἔοικε δέ πως … εὐδοκιμήσεις) is finished by the first three words of section 9 (ἡμῖν τῶν ἁγίων ὑποδηλοῦν); the whole sentence is rendered here so the reading text does not break mid-clause, and section 9’s English begins with the next sentence (Κλίβανος γάρ). ‘Do not grumble’ (μὴ γογγύζετε) matches 1 Corinthians 10:10 word for word (μηδὲ γογγύζετε), not Philippians 2:14. ‘The priest will offer up its memorial portion’ recalls Leviticus 2:2 (just quoted in section 7); the verb ἀνοίσει is closest to Leviticus 2:16. Θεῷ καὶ Πατρί rendered ‘God the Father’. Ἐν γνώσει Θεοῦ γεγόναμεν is ambiguous (‘come into the knowledge of God’ or ‘come to be in God’s knowledge’); rendered ‘come to be known by God’ because the context is God’s remembrance of us (compare Galatians 4:9, not cited). The quotation joins Leviticus 2:4–7 and 2:14–16, skipping 2:8–13, and omits the pouring of oil in 2:15 (καὶ ἐπιχεεῖς ἐπ’ αὐτὴν ἔλαιον); the source switches person (‘you … his … your’) as printed. Source πεπιλημένην (‘pressed’) is almost certainly a misprint or variant for the LXX πεπεμμένην (‘baked’); rendered ‘baked’. Χίδρα ἐρικτά, LXX ‘groats crushed’; Cyril himself glosses it as meal from pulse (ἐξ ὀσπρίων ἄλευρον). Ἥκιστα μὲν ἐκ πυρῶν, ‘least of all from wheat’, rendered ‘even if it is not of wheat at all’. Matthew 10:42 as quoted adds ἀδελφῶν (‘brothers’), probably from Matthew 25:40; cited only to 10:42. The lawgiver here is God (He accepts the gift), so ‘Lawgiver’ is capitalized; φησίν in the paraphrase of the law is rendered ‘the law says’.

title: Oven and grill mean trial; the unblemished calf of the peace offering
english: Cyril: For the oven and the grill, and also being ground fine in a mill, would surely be signs of the crushing and toil of those who are tested as if by fire. That is why those who walk so glorious a path cry out: ‘For you have tested us, O God; you have tried us by fire, as silver is tried by fire’ (Psalm 66:10). And the inspired David sings to us somewhere: ‘A crushed and humbled heart God will not despise’ (Psalm 51:17). But that those who have toiled in this way would fittingly, and in every respect, come to be in the fragrance of Christ (2 Corinthians 2:15), and indeed that they must also receive mercy and be richly nourished by the grace of the Spirit, would be plain to anyone who considers the use of the frankincense and the oil. Or are not the things in the law, in a way, hints and shadows of subtle riddles for us?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: So we shall offer ourselves to God, being made dead to sin and undergoing this sacred death in a spiritual sense, yet living to righteousness, as it is written (1 Peter 2:24), and rendering to him, as a kind of thank offering, our own life, glorious and blameless, and made beautiful by all that love for God can boast of. We shall learn this clearly from other laws as well. For it is written in Leviticus: ‘If his gift to the Lord is a sacrifice of salvation, if he offers it from the herd, whether male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the Lord. He shall lay his hands on the head of the gift and slaughter it before the Lord at the doors of the tent of witness. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall pour the blood on the altar of whole burnt offerings, all around. And from the sacrifice of salvation they shall bring as an offering to the Lord the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat that is on the entrails, and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is on the loins; and he shall remove the lobe of the liver together with the kidneys. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall carry them up to the altar, onto the whole burnt offerings, onto the wood that is on the fire on the altar; it is an offering, a fragrant aroma to the Lord’ (Leviticus 3:1–5).

The calf, then, is without blemish; for it is fitting that those who go up to God as a fragrant aroma should be pure and keep as far as they can from every blemish. It was slaughtered at the very doors of the holy tent, with the hands of the one offering it laid upon it; and what this means has been plainly stated already. The fat on the entrails was carried up for sacrifice, and the two kidneys, with the fat in them removed along with them, and the lobe of the liver. The fat on the entrails, I think, would signify the good health, so to speak, of the mind, and the richness of the inner parts when they have been nourished as well as can be on the spiritual provisions given through the Spirit. For good feeding makes brute animals, and human bodies too, grow fat; but a most abundant share in divine gifts fills the mind of the saints with every good thing.
translator_notes: PG 68.1025. Boundary in: the opening words ἡμῖν τῶν ἁγίων ὑποδηλοῦν finish the sentence that begins at the end of section 8 and are rendered there (‘the passage seems … to hint to us at the approval the saints win…’); this section’s English therefore starts with the next sentence. Boundary out: the last sentence (Θείων δὲ χαρισμάτων πλουσιωτάτη μέθεξις, παντὸς ἀγαθοῦ τὴν …) is finished by the first words of section 10 (τῶν ἁγίων ἐμπίπλησι φρένα) and is rendered whole here (‘fills the mind of the saints with every good thing’). LXX renumbering: Psalm 65:10 LXX = Psalm 66:10; Psalm 50:19 LXX = Psalm 51:17. Πυρόω rendered ‘tried by fire’ to keep Cyril’s link with the oven and the fire. ‘Come to be in the fragrance of Christ’ echoes 2 Corinthians 2:15 (Χριστοῦ εὐωδία ἐσμέν); cited as a clear allusion. ‘Living to righteousness’ (ζῶντες τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ) with κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον matches 1 Peter 2:24 (τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ ζήσωμεν); dying to sin also recalls Romans 6:11 and offering ourselves Romans 12:1, but those are left uncited as looser echoes. ‘Tested as if by fire’ may echo 1 Peter 1:7 and ‘shadows’ in the law Hebrews 10:1; both doubtful, uncited. Ἐλεεῖσθαι (‘receive mercy’) plays on ἔλαιον (‘oil’); the pun cannot be kept in English. Καταπιαίνεσθαι (literally ‘be fattened’) is rendered ‘be richly enriched’ of the Spirit’s grace and ‘grow fat’ of animals and bodies. Θυσία σωτηρίου, the LXX name for the peace offering, is kept as ‘sacrifice of salvation’ in the quotation; χαριστήρια rendered ‘thank offering’. Σκηνὴ τοῦ μαρτυρίου rendered ‘tent of witness’, as in sections 1–7. The law speaks of the herd (βόες); Cyril’s comment narrows it to ‘the calf’ (μόσχος). Κάρπωμα rendered ‘offering’ and ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας ‘a fragrant aroma’, matching sections 1–7. ‘What this means has been plainly stated already’ refers back to the laying on of hands discussed with the whole burnt offering earlier in the book.

title: Kidneys and liver: discernment and desire; each bears fruit by his measure
english: Cyril: So they would become holy, and set apart for God as a fragrant aroma. The kidneys, again, would be a type of the activity of discernment within the mind, by which one rejects what by nature does harm, and counts what is beneficial as worth choosing and taking. And the inspired Paul writes: ‘Test all things; hold fast what is good; keep away from every form of evil’ (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22). So since the kidney is a part of the body that discerns (for it separates out what is surplus very well, lets what is wholesome and useful into the body, and distributes it with art to the parts that should receive it, and in the right amount), we must with good reason take the kidneys to mean the discernment of the mind. Holy, then, and an offering dedicated to God are the kidneys of the saints, that is, the discernment they have in the mind. For those who cleave to God are approved and exact money changers: they always reject what is worthless as counterfeit, but they are accustomed to honor with their excellent verdict whatever leads to benefit. It was in this way, I think, that the inspired Psalmist, who was used to winning approval, cried out to God: ‘For you have taken possession of my kidneys, O Lord’ (Psalm 139:13).

The lobe of the liver, for its part, points us to nothing other than an activity of the soul, that is, a movement of the mind, by which it reaches out toward desires. Some who have studied such matters closely say without hesitation that every living creature has its desires in the liver. So the lobe of the liver too must be dedicated to God, that is, so to speak, the very source of all our desire, as the Psalmist sings: ‘Lord, all my desire is before you’ (Psalm 38:9). And a person takes pride in himself and sings out so solemn and admirable a word if his longings are set on nothing but what pleases God, and he is found thirsting for whatever he himself may wish to do.
Palladius: I agree; you understand it rightly.

Cyril: For the sheep, in turn, and for the goat as well, the Lawgiver lays down the same law, and the sacrifice was carried out in the same way for these too (Leviticus 3:6–16). The difference in size among the animals neatly points to the measure of piety and approval among those who are used to bearing fruit. For one person, we should think, bears fruit richly and above the rest, as in the calf; another moderately, as in the sheep; and another more modestly still, for a goat is smaller than a sheep. And this, I think, is the fruitful earth yielding a hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold, as in the parable in the Gospels (Matthew 13:8).
Palladius: I am convinced.

Cyril: That the repayment of reward will be in proportion to each one’s good deeds, and that God will allot to those who have chosen to act nobly rewards matched to their labors, the Savior himself will assure us. He says that the talents were not handed out in equal shares (Matthew 25:15), and of those who did well he sets one over ten cities and another over five (Luke 19:17–19). For each one’s life is weighed, as it were, in the balance, and the repayment will surely be equal in weight to our goodness.
translator_notes: PG 68.1028. Boundary in: the opening words τῶν ἁγίων ἐμπίπλησι φρένα complete the last sentence of section 9 and are rendered there; this section’s English starts with Τοιγάρτοι. Boundary out: the section ends inside the word ἀντέκτι|σις (‘repayment’), finished by the syllable σις that opens section 11; the whole word is rendered here, so section 11 starts with οὐδὲν δὲ ἧττον (‘and no less…’). The subject of ‘they would become holy’ is the saints whose minds are filled with good (end of section 9); ἐξαίρετοι (‘choice, set apart’) may also play on ἐξαιρέω, the removing of the fat. LXX renumbering: Psalm 138:13 LXX = Psalm 139:13 (Hebrew-based Bibles read ‘you formed my inward parts’; the LXX ἐκτήσω ‘took possession of’ and νεφροί ‘kidneys’ are kept because Cyril’s argument rests on them); Psalm 37:10 LXX = Psalm 38:9. ‘Approved money changers’ (δόκιμοι τραπεζῖται) echoes the well-known unwritten saying ‘Be approved money changers’, found in many early writers but not in the canonical Gospels; no citation given. The view that the desires lodge in the liver is Platonic (Timaeus 70d–72b) and widespread in ancient medicine; Cyril names no source. Ὧδε … εὐδοκιμεῖν εἰωθότα is rendered ‘It was in this way … that the inspired Psalmist, who was used to winning approval, cried out’; it could also mean that his approval came from this kind of discernment. Ἃ ἂν βούλοιτο δρᾶν αὐτός is ambiguous: αὐτός may be God (‘whatever he himself may wish to do’, adopted, since the clause before speaks of what pleases God) or the person (‘what he himself would want to do’). Ἐπὶ προβάτῳ … καὶ αἰγί refers to Leviticus 3:6–11 (sheep) and 3:12–16 (goat); the subject of ὁρίζει is the Lawgiver, made explicit in English. The order hundred, sixty, thirty matches Matthew 13:8 (and 13:23), not Mark 4:8. Cyril joins two parables: the unequal talents (Matthew 25:15) and the rule over ten and five cities, which belongs to the parable of the pounds (Luke 19:17–19). Ταλαντεύεται (‘is weighed’) plays on τάλαντα (‘talents’); the pun is lost in English. Ἐπιείκειαι rendered ‘goodness’, as in section 4.

title: Offerings that grow with the size of the victim
english: Cyril: …and no less, as I said, the law given through Moses will itself show us this. For it says again in Numbers: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you enter the land where you are to dwell, which I am giving you, and you make burnt offerings to the Lord, a whole offering or a sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering, or at your feasts, to make a fragrant aroma for the Lord, whether from the herd or from the flock, then the one who offers shall bring his gift to the Lord: an offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil; and you shall prepare a quarter of a hin of wine for a drink offering with the burnt offering or with the sacrifice. For each lamb you shall do this much, an offering by fire, a fragrant aroma for the Lord. And for a ram, when you prepare it as a burnt offering or as a sacrifice, you shall prepare an offering of two tenths of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil; and you shall bring a third of a hin of wine for a drink offering, as a fragrant aroma for the Lord. And if you prepare one from the herd as a burnt offering or as a sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or as a peace offering to the Lord, then with the calf one shall bring an offering of three tenths of fine flour mixed with half a hin of oil, and half a hin of wine for a drink offering, an offering by fire as a fragrant aroma for the Lord. So you shall do for each calf, or for each ram, or for each lamb from the sheep or from the goats. According to the number that you prepare, so you shall do for each one, according to their number. Every native-born person shall do so when he brings such offerings by fire as a fragrant aroma for the Lord. And if a proselyte joins you in your land, or whoever may be among you throughout your generations, and he makes an offering by fire as a fragrant aroma for the Lord, as you do, so shall the congregation do for the Lord. There shall be one law for you and for the proselytes who have joined you, a perpetual law throughout your generations; as you are, so shall the proselyte be before the Lord. There shall be one law and one ordinance for you and for the proselyte who has joined you.’ (Numbers 15:1–16)
Palladius: Then where in all this are we to see, as you put it, a share equal and proportionate to whatever a person does?

Cyril: Why, my friend, do you not hear the law saying plainly that if someone chooses to fulfill vows and burnt offerings, and he sacrifices a lamb, he is to add to what is burned a tenth of an ephah of fine flour and a quarter of a hin of wine and of oil? (These, I believe, are Hebrew measures.) But if it is a ram, it says, the accompanying portions come in greater amount, that is, a third; for the measure of a quarter is less than a third. And when a calf is offered, the fine flour and the rest go beyond the third once more, and come at last to a half.
Palladius: I have learned that. What, then, does it mean?
Cyril: You surely know that fine wheat flour is a type of life, and the oil a type of cheerfulness; for it is written,
translator_notes: Opens on the tail '-σις' of ἀντέκτισις ('repayment'), whose sentence begins in §10; that word is left to §10 and only the following clause is translated here (marked with an ellipsis). Quotation is LXX Numbers 15:1–16 (verse 16 ends with 'the proselyte who has joined you'). μεγαλύναι εὐχήν (literally 'to magnify a vow') rendered 'to fulfill a vow'; σωτήριον rendered 'peace offering'; κάρπωμα 'offering by fire'; θυσία σεμιδάλεως 'offering of fine flour'; μόσχος 'calf' to match Cyril's own summary. In his summary Cyril gives the wine and oil fractions (quarter, third, half) and for the calf loosely says the fine flour 'and the rest' go beyond a third; he does not mention the flour going from one to two to three tenths. Translated as he wrote it, not corrected. θυμίαμα in 'add to what is burned' is the burnt offering's smoke, not incense here. Speaker label: the print marks the fourth turn 'Ἐπυθόμην· τί οὖν τοῦτό γε;' as {ΚΥΡ.}, but it answers Cyril and is followed by another Cyril turn, so it is given to Palladius; this differs from the printed edition. Ends mid-word 'γέ|γραπται': 'for it is written' is finished here and the quotation follows at the head of §12. 'Fine flour = life' may glance at the bread of life (John 6:35) but Cyril does not say so; uncited.

title: Different glory, one way for all
english: Cyril: …‘to make the face cheerful with oil’ (Psalm 104:15). And the wine is a sign of spiritual gladness, the gladness that comes from above and through the Spirit; for ‘wine,’ it says, ‘gladdens the human heart’ (Psalm 104:15).
Palladius: I understand.

Cyril: So then, in proportion to the fruit someone bears, the supply of life from God also comes, with cheerfulness and gladness. Of course we do not say that in living itself, that is, in being given life by God, there is a greater or a lesser; for that is nonsense. When we speak of life, we mean the splendor that belongs to living, in which one person may perhaps surpass another, while another, again, will stand lower than others, yet not without honor and glory; ‘for star differs from star in glory’ (1 Corinthians 15:41). Here too, then, the difference among the victims is an image of the saints’ life in glory: by the quantity of the portions that go with each, it sketches for us the measure of that glory. And that those from the nations, together with those of Israel’s blood, would bow their necks under the Savior’s yoke, and go by way of the same sacrifices and the same spiritual excellence, the law showed when it added that the proselyte is not to live by other laws. For there is one way for all into kinship with God the Father, and that way is Christ (John 14:6). For as the inspired Peter said, ‘There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved’ (Acts 4:12).
Palladius: Our argument has turned out excellently, and with great skill.

Cyril: That we shall not be speaking falsely in the least when we affirm that there are different kinds of excellence, and that God will assign rewards matched in weight to each one’s measure, the most wise Paul will also make clear when he says: ‘Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully’ (2 Corinthians 9:6). And long before, David too had cried out: ‘And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the cleanness of my hands he will repay me’ (Psalm 18:20). Or would you not say that the righteousness of Paul, for example, is different from that of anyone at all who has not yet reached the stature we may picture in Paul (I mean in spiritual strength), a stature that enabled him to cry out plainly: ‘But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ (Galatians 6:14)?
Palladius: Certainly.
Cyril: What then? Shall we not grant that the cleanness of John’s hands is different from that of someone else who is just springing up to make a start in the Gospel way of life?
Palladius: We shall grant it; how could we not?

Cyril: Then tell me: since the Judge of all is just, will he demand from us a righteousness that keeps pace with the excellence of the saints and is like it in every way? Or rather, having tested the measure of strength within us, will he demand nothing more than what a person has and is able to accomplish?
translator_notes: Both oil and wine quotations are LXX Psalm 103:15 = English Psalm 104:15. David's quotation is LXX Psalm 17:21 = English Psalm 18:20 (the same words recur at Psalm 18:24 and 2 Samuel 22:21; Cyril's word order, with 'He will repay me' at the end, matches Psalm 18:20). Galatians 6:14 is quoted without 'our Lord Jesus' as Cyril gives it. ἐπ' εὐλογίαις in 2 Corinthians 9:6 (literally 'with blessings') rendered 'bountifully', the usual sense. 'One way ... and that way is Christ' is cited to John 14:6 as a clear allusion (way + access to the Father). Uncited allusions: 'the Savior's yoke' may echo Matthew 11:29–30; 'the Judge of all' may echo Genesis 18:25; neither is clear enough to cite. νοητή εὐφρασία rendered 'spiritual gladness' (gladness of the mind, not of the senses). εὐδοκίμησις rendered 'excellence' throughout. 'John' is not identified by Cyril (the Baptist or the apostle); left as 'John'. The John turn ends with a comma in the print; read as a question. In the last turn ἤγουν is taken as 'or rather', setting two alternatives; Palladius's reply in §13 takes the second.

title: God asks according to each one’s means
english: Palladius: I say so myself. For Christ said this: ‘From the one to whom they have entrusted much, they will ask much’ (Luke 12:48). And clearly the reverse is also true: surely little will be asked of the one who has received less.

Cyril: Look, then, at the matter as it is written in the law, and see God asking of each in proportion to each one’s measure. Being the spring and source of a gentleness and love for humankind beyond words, he sends away none of those who have run to him through faith; he welcomes each with whatever he has, and accepts spiritual offerings, in every case excusing what lies beyond a person’s strength. The law on this point reads as follows in Leviticus: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: If anyone makes a vow to give the Lord the value of his own life, the valuation of a male from twenty years old to sixty years old shall be this: his valuation shall be fifty didrachms of silver by the holy weight; and for a female the valuation shall be thirty didrachms. If from five years old to twenty years, the valuation of a male shall be twenty didrachms, and of a female ten didrachms. From one month old to five years old, the valuation of a male shall be five didrachms of silver, and of a female three didrachms of silver. And from sixty years old and upward, if it is a male, his valuation shall be fifteen didrachms of silver, and if a female, ten didrachms of silver. But if he is too poor for the valuation, he shall stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him; according to what the hand of the one who vowed can afford, so the priest shall value him’ (Leviticus 27:1–8). For some came forward, enrolling themselves with God for consecration and as an offering dedicated to him, and gladly dedicating the sum of didrachms the law had fixed. But if someone was not very well off, that is, one of the humbler sort, the payment was no longer made by the legal scale; instead the priest serving at the time assessed him, and a debt matched to his means was set. This, then, is the plainer account and sense of the letter. But I think it necessary to remind those who attend to the sacred words with the greatest love of learning that Christ, speaking once to the Pharisees, called this very commandment to mind clearly and plainly. For they had turned aside into a debased way of life, one the law did not recognize, and were ‘teaching as doctrines the commandments of men,’ as it is written (Matthew 15:9; Isaiah 29:13), and they came to him saying: ‘Why do your disciples transgress the commandment of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread’ (Matthew 15:2). At once the Savior said to them: ‘Why do you also transgress the commandment of God? For God said, Honor your father and your mother, that it may be well with you (Exodus 20:12). But you say, Whoever says to his father and his mother, “Whatever help you might have had from me is a gift,” shall not honor his father and his mother. And you have made void the commandment of God for the sake of…’ (Matthew 15:3–6)
translator_notes: Luke 12:48 is quoted loosely (Cyril has ζητήσουσι παρ' αὐτοῦ where Luke has περισσότερον αἰτήσουσιν αὐτόν in the second half). Leviticus 27:1–8 is LXX, where 'shekel' is rendered δίδραχμον ('didrachm'); kept as 'didrachms'. τιμὴ τῆς ψυχῆς rendered 'the value of his own life' (ψυχή = the person vowed). 'Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men' follows the word order of Matthew 15:9 (= Mark 7:7), which quotes LXX Isaiah 29:13; both cited. Matthew 15:2 is quoted with 'commandment of the elders' where Matthew has 'tradition of the elders', and Cyril's Matthew 15:3 lacks 'because of your tradition'; translated as Cyril gives them. 'That it may be well with you' is not in Matthew 15:4; Cyril adds it from LXX Exodus 20:12 (also Deuteronomy 5:16), hence the Exodus citation. οὐ μὴ τιμήσει (emphatic future negative) kept as 'shall not honor'; in Matthew it means the vow frees the son from honoring his parents. The section ends mid-phrase 'διὰ τὴν | παράδοσιν ὑμῶν' ('for the sake of | your tradition'); 'your tradition' falls at the head of §14. Possible but uncited echoes: 'He sends away none who have run to him' (John 6:37); 'spiritual gifts' (1 Peter 2:5, spiritual sacrifices).

title: The Pharisees’ ‘gift’, and the life we owe to Christ
english: Cyril: …because of your tradition’ (Matthew 15:6). For the Pharisees, being greatly in love with money and greedy for gain, wanted to see as many people as possible coming to the enrollment the law prescribed, so that their purses might grow fat as they gathered with insatiable hand what came from each one who approached. But it was likely that some would hold back from the enrollment, having their poverty as an honorable excuse for hesitating, and above all the duty of caring in old age for their fathers or mothers out of what they themselves earned, and that with no little sweat. No sooner had the wicked Pharisees learned this than they urged them to go readily to the dedication. They no longer thought as was right, and they set aside what the law had laid down, I mean, that reverence toward parents be shown in full and that they be treated with tender care; instead they urged them, so to speak, to bid a quick farewell to fulfilling what custom required. For since under the laws it was a crime and an indictable offense to take for oneself anything that had been offered for the glory of God, and ‘gift’ was the name given to dedicated offerings, they taught people to say to their own parents, when they asked for support: ‘Whatever you might have gained from me is a gift’ (Matthew 15:5). That is: whatever I might give you is a dedicated offering, and be sure that you would be wronging the law, stealing what belongs to the glory of God and taking it impiously. And the men who brought in these most shameful inventions of theirs affirmed that inhumanity toward parents was blameless in those who had chosen instead to dedicate their goods to God according to the law. This, I think, is the meaning of the words: ‘Whoever says to his father or his mother, “Whatever you might have gained from me is a gift,” need not honor his father or his mother’ (Matthew 15:5–6). For the point is this: let those be allowed not to honor a father, nor to show reverence to a mother, who say, ‘Whatever you might have gained from me is a gift’; that is, whatever I might perhaps help you with by giving it to you, that is a gift to God, and you would be a thief of sacred offerings.
Palladius: That, I say, is rightly and truly said.
Cyril: Since the historical sense is now clear enough to us, let us go on to the spiritual meaning and take up the contemplation that goes beyond what the senses perceive.
Palladius: Let us go on.

Cyril: Every one of us, Palladius, who has been justified in faith and sanctified in the Spirit has become a sacred offering to God. Each of us owes his own life to Christ. For as the inspired Paul said, ‘We were bought with a price, and we are not our own’ (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). And, ‘One died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and was raised’ (2 Corinthians 5:14–15). For he acquired us through himself for God the Father, laying down his own blood as a kind of price on our behalf. So we come to Christ, the Savior of all, through faith and sanctification, bringing him a repayment for what he has done for us: the dedication of a life lived in godliness. Yet the manner of the offering may be understood, and with good reason, to be varied rather than one and the same. For some come to it without much strength, while others, with warmer…
translator_notes: PG 68.1036. Opens inside the quotation of Matthew 15:2–6 begun in §13; the surviving words (‘your tradition’) close Matthew 15:6. ‘Enrolment’ (ἀπογραφή) and ‘dedication’ (ἀνάθεσις) refer to the vow valuations of Leviticus 27 discussed in §13. Doubtful reading: ἐκτετιμηκότες normally means ‘having honored highly’, which contradicts the sense; the context requires ‘having set aside / slighted’ what the law decreed (most likely a misprint for ἐκτετμηκότες, ‘having cut out’, from ἐκτέμνω; less likely a form of ἀτιμάζω); rendered ‘set aside’. The accusative ἐπιφωνοῦντας is taken with the people the Pharisees urged, not with the Pharisees. The rule against appropriating sacred things is a general allusion to the law (compare Leviticus 5:15–16; Leviticus 27:28), too loose to cite. ‘We were bought with a price, and we are not our own’ adapts 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 (also 7:23) into the first person plural. ‘He acquired us through himself for God’ may echo Revelation 5:9; left uncited. Section ends mid-sentence (‘with warmer…’), continued in §15. οὐ μὴ τιμήσει is rendered ‘need not honor’, the sense Cyril himself draws out (‘let those be allowed not to honor’).

title: The ages of the vow as stages of the soul
english: Cyril: …zeal, as it were, rush toward it, and with a vigorous understanding, a wakeful mind and the strongest drive, they press on to accomplish whatever must be fulfilled, and to be able to carry out what is pleasing to him. According to what the history suggests, these would be the people from twenty years old up to sixty (Leviticus 27:3). For up to the sixtieth year the body stays strong and at its most vigorous in its movements. By then the mind, too, is settled and in a way strong, and it is very well suited to take in whatever it chooses to learn. And he who knows our frame, as it is written (Psalm 103:14), surely knew that there is such an age in souls also. For the passage, no doubt, moves, by likenesses drawn from bodily things, to the things perceived by the mind. So, whether one is male or female, let those who are still in the prime of that inward age bring what has been appointed. That is, let the male bring, in the form, as it were, of fifty didrachms, the fruit of spiritual worship, sound and as perfect as can be; for by way of seven times seven it is plainly seen to reach the highest goal and to be attested as perfect. The female, again, brings it in the form, as it were, of thirty didrachms (Leviticus 27:4). For she is held in less esteem than the male, yet she still brings, in keeping with her own nature, a fruit marked by perfection and toil, as the three tens suggest. The one from five years old up to twenty, if male, pays twenty didrachms; if female, ten (Leviticus 27:5). For from the age of five, I think, and barely then, the mind begins in a way to open its eyes, as it were, to understanding. That understanding is still childish and weak, but it is moving toward the better, and the body is growing ever stronger. Or do you not understand what I mean?
Palladius: Yes, very well.

Cyril: So the fruit from each person is measured in proportion to spiritual strength. Everywhere the female comes after the male, and often at half. For the inspired Paul has plainly testified that the vessel is weak (1 Peter 3:7). She falls short of the natural ability of men, and she keeps silent in the churches (1 Corinthians 14:34). For she has not been entrusted with the word, and she is by no means as strong for achieving virtue as the male is seen to be. From one month old, it says, up to five years, the male gives five didrachms, and the female, for her part, three (Leviticus 27:6). And yet what fruit could come from infants? So in a way the passage hints to us at the newborn child in Christ, those for whom, as the holy Paul said, milk is the fitting food (1 Corinthians 3:1–2). For the fruit of those who have only just been called through faith and are still infants is small. Knowing this, the inspired disciples, writing to those from the Gentiles, even though Christ had given a very great body of Gospel commandments, told them that they must keep themselves from fornication, from what is strangled and from blood; and they said that those who did these things would do well (Acts 15:28–29). For a mind that is still tender and childish must not be weighed down with very heavy burdens. The law added that from those sixty years old and over, fifteen didrachms must be required for a male and ten for a female (Leviticus 27:7). For what has already declined into feebleness and weakness…
translator_notes: PG 68.1037. Opens mid-sentence (‘with warmer zeal…’) from §14. τὸ αὐτῷ δοκοῦν is printed unaspirated; taken as ‘what is pleasing to him’ (God); αὑτῷ, ‘what seems good to himself’, is possible but less likely in context. ‘He who knows our frame’: LXX Psalm 102:14 (ἔγνω τὸ πλάσμα ἡμῶν) = English Psalm 103:14. ‘Seven times seven’: Cyril reads fifty as the completion that follows forty-nine. ‘The vessel is weak’ (τὸ σκεῦος ἀσθενές) is the wording of 1 Peter 3:7 (ἀσθενεστέρῳ σκεύει), which Cyril here attributes to Paul; the attribution is kept as he wrote it and the citation gives the actual verse. ‘She has not been entrusted with the word’ may echo 1 Timothy 2:12; left uncited. ‘Newborn child’ (ἀρτιγενές) may also echo 1 Peter 2:2; Cyril names Paul, so 1 Corinthians 3:1–2 is cited (compare Hebrews 5:12–13). The apostolic decree (fornication, what is strangled, blood; ‘you will do well’) is Acts 15:28–29 (also 15:20); ‘not be weighed down with heavy burdens’ echoes 15:28 and is covered by that citation. Cyril’s view of women is translated as he states it, without softening. Section ends mid-sentence, continued in §16. νοητῆς ἡλικίας is the ‘inward’ (mental) age, not πνευματικός; rendered ‘that inward age’. νηπιοπρεπῆ … ἰοῦσαν agree with σύνεσιν, so ‘childish and weak’ describes the understanding.

title: God accepts each by his strength; keep the vows you make
english: Cyril: …could hardly be very fruitful, just as aging plants, when their root grows old, are seen to be slow in putting forth ripe fruit. So God, who is truly just and loves to show compassion, accepts the fruits in proportion to each person’s zeal and capacity of mind. He neither disregards what is feeble and past its prime, sending it away as powerless, nor lets the strong go without reward; rather he opens wide, as it were, the way for those who are willing to win his approval, in whatever manner each is able. And those who are weaker in their condition, and perhaps also of little understanding, he himself will keep, measuring the fruit he asks of each by his strength. For this, I think, is the meaning of: ‘He shall stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him according to what the one who vowed can afford’ (Leviticus 27:8).
Palladius: How finely reasoned!

Cyril: So, Palladius, we must offer to God, like a sweet fragrance and as a debt we owe, a way of life fitting for saints and the glories of an outstanding life. You have learned from one of the saints, who wrote: ‘Honor the Lord from your just labors, and offer him firstfruits from your fruits of righteousness’ (Proverbs 3:9). For the people of old thought they honored him with sacrifices of oxen and with frankincense, since that was the road of life under the law. But we, who are now in Christ through faith, are going by the better and more excellent path, and we shall offer God worship in spirit and truth (John 4:23–24), making every effort, as it were, to be able to carry out nobly what we ought, and honoring God with spiritual and holy offerings. For I say that we must remember him who speaks plainly through the most wise Moses: ‘You shall keep what goes out through your lips’ (Deuteronomy 23:23). That is, whatever you vow, hasten to carry it out, and very promptly. For in such matters delay is not without loss. ‘For if you make a vow to the Lord,’ it says, ‘do not delay in paying it’ (Deuteronomy 23:21; Ecclesiastes 5:4). ‘It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay’ (Ecclesiastes 5:5).
Palladius: True.

Cyril: Indeed, there is a wise aim in the art of fulfilling vows and pledges as we ought, and one could learn it without error from no other source than the law. For it is written: ‘Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths’ (Psalm 119:105). Or are we not guided by the light of the divine law, and could one not speed along a straight road that never strays, with its rays as a kind of lamp?
Palladius: Of course. For the inspired David also sings somewhere: ‘The commandment of the Lord is radiant, giving light to the eyes’ (Psalm 19:8).

Cyril: You will learn very clearly how we shall win approval, living a glorious and wholly pure life and rendering to God, as a splendid offering, the ways of great goodness, for God gives us his charge through other oracles too.
translator_notes: PG 68.1040. Opens mid-sentence from §15 (‘what has already declined into feebleness…’). αὐτὸς ἕξει (‘He himself will have/hold’) is abrupt; rendered ‘He himself will keep’, meaning he keeps them in his acceptance; the text may be faulty. Palladius’s Ὡς ἰσχνὸς ὁ λόγος praises the argument as finely drawn (ἰσχνός, ‘slender, subtle’), not as weak. ‘Fragrant aroma’ (ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας) is stock sacrificial language (Leviticus passim; compare Ephesians 5:2, Philippians 4:18); no single verse is meant, so it is uncited. Proverbs 3:9 matches the LXX word for word. ‘Worship in Spirit and truth’ is the phrase of John 4:23–24 that gives the whole work its title. πάντα σείοντες κάλων is a proverb (‘shaking out every rope’), rendered by its sense ‘making every effort’. ‘You shall keep what goes out through your lips’: LXX Deuteronomy 23:24 = English Deuteronomy 23:23. The next quotation, introduced only by ‘it says’ after a mention of Moses, matches LXX Ecclesiastes 5:3–4 (μὴ χρονίσῃς τοῦ ἀποδοῦναι αὐτήν; ἀγαθὸν τὸ μὴ εὔξασθαί σε…) = English Ecclesiastes 5:4–5. The first clause blends LXX Deuteronomy 23:22 (= English 23:21: ἐὰν δὲ εὔξῃ εὐχὴν κυρίῳ, ‘if you vow a vow to the Lord’) with Ecclesiastes (μὴ χρονίσῃς τοῦ ἀποδοῦναι), so both are cited; the second sentence is Ecclesiastes 5:5 alone. LXX Psalm 118:105 reads ὁ λόγος σου (‘your word’); Cyril’s text has ὁ νόμος σου (‘your law’), and the English follows Cyril. ‘The commandment of the Lord is radiant’: LXX Psalm 18:9 = English Psalm 19:8. ἐπιείκεια rendered ‘goodness’ (moral excellence), its usual sense in Cyril. Lev 27:8 ‘the hand of the one who vowed’ is the Hebrew idiom for means; rendered ‘what the one who vowed can afford’.

title: Turning to the Nazirite vow in Numbers
english: Cyril: It reads like this in Numbers: ‘And the Lord spoke…’ (Numbers 6:1)
translator_notes: PG 68.1041. The section holds only the opening words of the quotation; the subject (Κύριος, ‘the Lord’) and the rest of the Nazirite law (Numbers 6:1–5 and following) fall in §18. ‘The Lord’ is moved into this section so the English reads naturally, and §18 begins ‘…to Moses, saying’.

title: The Nazirite vow, and the wine that clouds the mind
english: Cyril: ‘…to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and say to them: If a man or a woman makes a great vow to consecrate himself in purity to the Lord, he shall keep himself pure from wine and strong drink. He shall not drink vinegar made from wine or vinegar made from strong drink, nor drink anything that is made from grapes; he shall eat no fresh grapes or raisins all the days of the vow of his purification. Of all that comes from the vine, wine from the pressed skins down to the seed, he shall eat nothing all the days of his purification. No razor shall come upon his head until the days are fulfilled that he vowed to the Lord. He shall be holy, letting the locks of the hair of his head grow, all the days of the vow to the Lord. He shall not go near any dead person, not to his father or his mother, nor to his brother or his sister; he shall not be defiled for them when they die, because the vow of his God is upon him, upon his head. All the days of his vow he shall be holy to the Lord. And if anyone dies suddenly beside him, at once the head of his vow shall be defiled; and he shall shave his head on the day he is cleansed; on the seventh day he shall be shaved. And on the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest, to the doors of the tent of witness. And the priest shall offer one for sin and one as a whole burnt offering, and the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin he committed in the matter of the dead; and he shall sanctify his head on that day, the day on which he consecrated all the days of his vow to the Lord. And he shall bring a year-old lamb as a whole burnt offering for the trespass. And the former days shall not count, because the head of his vow was defiled’ (Numbers 6:1–12).

Palladius: This oracle is not easy to understand; indeed, it can hardly be understood at all unless the law is examined closely. Not cutting the hair, but letting it grow long and hang loose, and keeping away from wine and vinegar and raisins, and even from grape seeds: what kind of worship could there be in that?

Cyril: None at all, Palladius, in truth, if one looks simply at the practice itself, at what it is by nature. Yet the aim of the law is admirable. It skillfully recasts the customs of the Greeks into something more seemly, and gracefully turns even what seems pointless into an image of the Gospel life. So if anyone aims to consecrate himself to God by the great vow, that is, by the highest way of life and the straight and blameless path of perfect righteousness, let wine and strong drink be far from him; that is, let him free his mind from everything that can make it drunk and that tends to cloud it. These, I think, would be a worldly outlook, earthly desires, the cares of the flesh and idle distractions. It was for falling into these that a prophetic word lamented some of the priests, saying something like this: ‘For priest and prophet were beside themselves because of wine, from the drunkenness of strong drink’ (Isaiah 28:7). And indeed about others too the…
translator_notes: Column join with §17: §17 ends «Καὶ ἐλάλησε and §18 begins Κύριος πρὸς Μωσῆν λέγων. English word order needs the subject with the verb, so 'the Lord' is rendered in §17 ('And the Lord spoke'), and §18 begins '…to Moses, saying'. The Nazirite law is Numbers 6:1–12 LXX; Cyril's text has 'whole burnt offering of trespass' (ὁλοκαύτωμα πλημμελείας) in 6:12 where the standard LXX reads 'for a trespass offering'; translated as Cyril has it. 'ἄλογοι' rendered 'shall not count' (the days are void). Masculine 'he' kept after 'a man or a woman' as the Greek does. Palladius' 'ἥκιστά γε μήν, οὐχὶ τοῦ νόμου λεπτὴν παθόντος τὴν βάσανον' taken as 'hardly at all, unless the law is examined closely'; the elliptical construction is doubtful.
