Isaiah 28:7 LXX verified (ἱερεὺς καὶ προφήτης ἐξέστησαν διὰ τὸν οἶνον... ἀπὸ τῆς μέθης τοῦ σίκερα). Sentence breaks off at 'the' and continues with 'prophet says' in §19.

title: A pagan custom turned to good: hair as the fruit of the mind
english: Cyril: …prophet says: ‘For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their tendril from Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, theirs is a cluster of bitterness; their wine is the rage of dragons’ (Deuteronomy 32:32–33). And some others are said to give their neighbor a muddy draught that overturns him (Habakkuk 2:15). So the law shuts the mind of the consecrated away from everything apt to make it drunk. And it says, very rightly, that they must have no share in vinegar either; by vinegar, I think, it means pleasures that are against nature and perverted. It forbids the use of raisins and grape seeds, not allowing the mind to stoop in the least to the old remnants of the pleasures within us. Wine, then, and all that comes from it, has been condemned by the law for this reason, I think, and for no other. Next, what might the command to let the hair grow long for God mean? Come, let us explain it, once I have first stated one point ahead of the rest. The most senseless of the Greeks, following unnatural customs and living like irrational beasts, used to let their hair grow, claiming that they grew it for demons. One would cut it off for the mountain nymphs, another for a river, at set times; and this practice was a form of worship for them. But Moses in his great wisdom, or rather the all-wise God, the finest of craftsmen, through Moses, gave the Israelites laws of the same kind, since the error of Egypt was hard for them to wash away. He moved them little by little by means of their ancient habits and ways, so that they would no longer offer their reverence to demons, but to the God of all, by way of type and shadow. That is why he also laid down the laws about the sacrifices, and accepted the sacrifices of blood against his will. Indeed he said plainly through the voice of Isaiah: ‘For who required these things from your hands?’ (Isaiah 1:12). So among the Greeks the custom was utterly irrational; but the law teaches what is better, and by reason sets in good order even what seems pointless. Would you like us, as far as we can, to speak about each point in turn?
Palladius: Very much so.
Cyril: Or do you not know (for I will remind you) that the word made the head a type of the mind, as the mind’s dwelling place? For this is how the inspired Scripture takes it.
Palladius: I agree. What of it, then?

Cyril: This: hairs are the fruits of the head, and they spring up like shoots native to it; and thoughts, and all that comes from the mind, would in turn be the mind’s fruit, welling up in us in the same way, and adorning it, as it were, like a fine and flourishing head of hair. So we must not keep the mind within us bare and stripped of good thoughts, but rather teeming, as it were, and growing its hair long for God with an exact knowledge of every excellent thing. Through this knowledge it will search out the divine beauty itself, whatever it may be, and clearly survey the things hidden as in the depths, and grow rich in thoroughly sound reasoning, so as to be able to gain a wholly blameless knowledge of God and to walk a path entirely free from error: the path, I mean, toward all that is admirable. Or would you not say that such a person is already, in a way, speeding on to the portion…
translator_notes: Opening continues the sentence begun at the end of §18 ('the prophet says'); Cyril calls Moses 'the prophet' for the Song of Deuteronomy 32. Deuteronomy 32:32–33 LXX verified ('θυμὸς δρακόντων ὁ οἶνος αὐτῶν'); Cyril has 'βότρυς πικρίας αὐτῶν' for LXX 'αὐτοῖς'. Habakkuk 2:15 LXX ('ὁ ποτίζων τὸν πλησίον αὐτοῦ ἀνατροπῇ θολερᾷ') is paraphrased, so it is cited as an allusion. Isaiah 1:12 LXX verified. 'νόμον ἡμῖν ἀναβρύουσαι' is doubtful: taken as adverbial νόμον ('in the same way', i.e. like hairs), not 'welling up a law for us'; the print may be corrupt. 'ἐκεῖνο τῶν ἄλλων προηγορευκότες' read as 'first stating one point before the rest' (the Greek background that follows). 'θεόπνευστος Γραφή' is a standard term; no citation of 2 Timothy 3:16 given. The subject of 'bars', 'says' and 'forbids' is the lawgiver; English uses 'the law', which is named in the same passage. Final question breaks at 'λῆξιν'; 'of all praise' continues in §20.

title: A shaven head and a bare mind; God above family ties
english: Cyril: …of all praise?
Palladius: Certainly.
Cyril: And what of this? Would not shaving and stripping the head bare, with the hair cut close to the skin, bring an impression of dishonor on anyone to whom it might happen?
Palladius: I understand.

Cyril: For if God says to the mother of the Jews, I mean Jerusalem, ‘Shave and shear yourself for your delicate children; make your widowhood wide like an eagle, because they have been taken captive from you’ (Micah 1:16), it is because shaving brings insult and dishonor, and is most fitting for those who mourn.
Palladius: You have spoken well.

Cyril: Bare, then, and utterly dishonored, and full of shame is the mind that does not have within itself the things that make it admirable. Among such would quite rightly be counted those of little understanding, and those who hold a corrupt opinion of God, so as to worship stones, that is, to dare senselessly to give reverence to the creation rather than to the Creator and Maker (Romans 1:25), and to think and say what is wholly perverse, and to shake off the true and blameless faith, and instead to leap at whatever anyone might blurt out in folly, because their mind has no full head of good thoughts.
Palladius: Excellently said.

Cyril: Let the mind, then, be filled with thoughts that lead to rightness, and be crowned, as with a head of hair, with the discoveries of reflection on everything admirable. Such a person is as sensible as can be, and well fitted from now on to receive into himself the enlightenment that is in Christ through faith. As for the one so well endowed, who has trained himself in an exceptional life and is distinguished by such a mind, the divine oracle commands him to keep far from everything that by its nature defiles, to withdraw from fleshly deeds, and to cast as far away as possible whatever tends toward deadness and corruption. So the rule that one must not visit the dead, nor be willing to be defiled over a corpse, surely hints at this for us. The law bars him from such things entirely, setting what pleases God above reverence for parents. ‘For he shall not go near,’ it says, ‘his father or his mother’ (Numbers 6:6–7). For when virtue is being achieved, away with love of the flesh; let God hold the first and higher place over kinship by blood. This is what Christ himself also said: ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10:37–38). The Savior himself also taught us that the things of God rank above reverence for parents. For there came to him one of those already counted…
translator_notes: Opens with the end of the question begun in §19 ('the portion of all praise?'). The print reads 'τεμνομένης ἐν Χριστῷ τῆς τριχός' with the marginal correction γρ. Χρωτί; 'ἐν Χριστῷ' makes no sense here and 'ἐν χρωτί' is the idiom for cutting close to the skin, so the correction is followed. Micah 1:16 LXX verified (ξύρησαι καὶ κεῖραι ἐπὶ τὰ τέκνα τὰ τρυφερά σου, ἐμπλάτυνον τὴν χηρείαν σου ὡς ἀετός). The 'For if God says…' sentence has no main clause in the Greek; English supplies 'it is because' to join it to the next sentence. 'παρὰ τὸν κτίστην' follows Romans 1:25 (τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα), a clear allusion. Numbers 6:6–7 cited for 'He shall not go in… to a father or to a mother'. Matthew 10:37–38 verified; Cyril has 'ὁ φιλῶν… ὑπὲρ ἐμέ' and 'λαμβάνει'. 'σαρκικῶν ἔργων' rendered 'fleshly works' and left uncited: it is not the wording of Galatians 5:19. φωτισμός ('enlightenment') may carry a baptismal sense. Last sentence breaks at 'τῶν ἤδη τελούντων'; 'among the disciples' continues in §21.

title: Defiled by the dead: lost days, and cleansing in Christ
english: Cyril: …among the disciples, saying: ‘Lord, let me first go and bury my father.’ But he said, ‘Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead’ (Matthew 8:21–22). By ‘the dead’, I think, he means those who have chosen to set their minds on the things of the world and have not kept away from the deeds of death.
Palladius: So it is.

Cyril: This, then, is the manner of the wholly pure and exceptional way of life according to the law, or rather as it is in spirit and truth (John 4:23–24); for the law is a shadow (Hebrews 10:1). But if it should happen, it says, that the consecrated person is ever defiled over a dead body, let him then be shorn and have his head stripped bare, since his hair has now in a way become unholy. And on the eighth day he shall bring a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. And let him also bring, it says, a year-old lamb; and the first days shall not count, because the head of his vow was defiled (Numbers 6:9–12). For if the consecrated person should grow careless of what is fitting and be defiled by ways that lead to deadness, having turned aside to the things of the flesh, it will surely follow that he must barter away the glories of the wholly pure way of life, and he will make his own head, as it were, utterly dishonored. For the shaving hints at something of this kind. And having labored in vain through the time that is past, he will lament the loss of his sweat. This, I think, is the meaning of ‘The first days shall not count.’ He says something like this through the voice of Ezekiel too: ‘The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on the day he sins; and the lawlessness of the lawless shall not harm him on the day he turns from his lawlessness’ (Ezekiel 33:12). So if the consecrated should somehow be defiled in the meantime, they will suffer the loss of what they had already achieved; yet the loss they suffer from it is not hard to escape. For they are scoured clean in Christ, who, in the place, as it were, of the turtledove and the dove, offers himself for us to God the Father, and is sacrificed as a lamb, and justifies us by the death of his own flesh. That is why the law has ordered that the one who has undergone the shaving should offer sacrifices as a type of Christ, who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), strengthens what is weak, raises what has fallen, turns back what has strayed (Ezekiel 34:16), and washes clean what has been stained.
Palladius: Excellently said.

Cyril: But I think that if we apply our minds a little to what lies before us, we can see another depth of subtle and hidden ideas. For the law, not without forethought, spurs us toward this very thing when it speaks of the one who grows his hair for God: ‘But if one dies suddenly, at once the head of his vow shall be defiled; and he shall shave his head on the day he is cleansed; on the seventh day he shall be shaved. And on the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest. And he shall sanctify,’ it says, ‘his head on that day’ (Numbers 6:9–11). He was also commanded to offer a year-old lamb (Numbers 6:12).
Palladius: One taught by Christ might well be at a loss to know what, then, the riddle means. I am eager to learn: tell me what it points to.
translator_notes: Opens by continuing the sentence from §20 ('one of those already counted among the disciples'). Matthew 8:21–22 verified (ἐπίτρεψόν μοι πρῶτον ἀπελθεῖν καὶ θάψαι τὸν πατέρα μου); the parallel is Luke 9:59–60, but the wording is Matthew's. 'In spirit and truth' alludes to John 4:23–24, the phrase in the title of the work; lowercase 'spirit' follows the majority use in the other Books. 'σκιὰ γὰρ ὁ νόμος' follows Hebrews 10:1 (also compare Colossians 2:17). The Numbers 6:9–12 paraphrase in the first long turn is Cyril's own summary; 'ἄλογοι' rendered 'shall not count'. Ezekiel 33:12 LXX verified; Cyril has 'ἐν ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἁμάρτῃ' where the LXX has 'πλανηθῇ' (compare Ezekiel 18:24–27). 'δικαιοῦντος τὸν ἀσεβῆ' is Romans 4:5 word for word. 'ἐπιστρέφοντος τὸ πλανώμενον' matches Ezekiel 34:16 LXX (τὸ πλανώμενον ἐπιστρέψω), and 'strengthens what is weak' echoes Ezekiel 34:4/16 more loosely; one citation is placed after the shepherd series. 'Offers himself for us to God the Father' may echo Ephesians 5:2 or Hebrews 9:14; left uncited as doubtful. 'Works of deadness' (νεκρότητος ἔργα) may echo Hebrews 6:1 and 9:14 ('dead works'); left uncited. 'προστέταχε' has no expressed subject; English gives 'the law', which is the subject of the next commands. In the final quotation the Greek 'Ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ ἐξάπινα' has no 'τις'; rendered 'if one dies' to keep the subject open, since the riddle Palladius asks about turns on it.

title: Hair as the mind’s thoughts: Israel’s vow, and the shaving before the eighth day
english: Cyril: Then I will tell you as best I can. But you, for your part, must forgive me if I stray at all from the road; for the subject is a subtle one, and the riddle obscure.
Palladius: Agreed.

Cyril: Since the head of the body, Palladius, represents in itself the mind for us (for so the divine and holy Scripture saw fit), we liken to hairs and locks the thoughts that rise naturally from the mind and within it, by which we are guided to the knowledge of anything that exists, whatever it may be. For these are what spring up for us from the head.
Palladius: I will keep that in mind.

Cyril: So in us too the mind is, in a manner of speaking, unshorn, and has a full head of hair for God, when it is filled with good thoughts. But it is bare and stripped, and suffers a most shameful baldness, if it neither holds right conceptions of God nor is enriched with the best and blameless knowledge of all that ought to be done.
Palladius: True; we were going over this just now.

Cyril: So then, before the coming of the Savior, Israel was called through Moses to the knowledge of God, and for this reason he was also sanctified. And in a certain way he made to God the vow of purity. For at Mount Horeb he plainly promised that he would keep the law, saying: ‘All that the Lord God has spoken we will do and hear’ (Exodus 24:7; Deuteronomy 5:27). So his mind was full of the teaching of the law, and the glories of the commandment given through Moses were, as it were, a head of hair grown for God. But they were defiled by a dead body, for they killed Emmanuel. The death of Christ was truly holy, but for those who killed him the guilt of killing the Lord was a defilement. So the law now commands them to shave off the teaching of the law like a head of hair, and, one might almost say, to crop off on the seventh day whatever was in types (Numbers 6:9), that is, whatever came before the eighth day, the day on which Christ came back to life, renewing us to incorruption and refashioning us for a new life, the life of the Gospel. So, having cropped off what came before the eighth day, he grows his hair again and sanctifies his head after the eighth day (Numbers 6:11). And the mind grows its hair again no longer with types and shadows, as before, but with the very teachings that stand in faith and truth. Or do you not think that those justified by faith must be stripped, as it were, of the good repute won by worship under the law, and must grow anew and take into their inmost mind and heart the knowledge of the Gospel way of life, as far better and more excellent than the way given at the beginning?
Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: Did not Paul, a man schooled in the law, cry out clearly and openly about those ancient glories of the law, saying: ‘Whatever things were gain to me, these I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. More than that, I count all things as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Jesus Christ our Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I count them…’ (Philippians 3:7–8)
translator_notes: Section opens with Cyril’s reply to Palladius’ question at the end of §21. Promise at Horeb: Cyril’s wording has the order ποιήσομεν καὶ ἀκουσόμεθα of Exodus 24:7 LXX (‘we will do and hear’, said at Sinai), while ‘Lord God’ and the name Horeb match Deuteronomy 5:27 (Deuteronomy calls Sinai Horeb, 5:2); both cited; compare also Exodus 19:8 and 24:3. ‘On the seventh day’ and ‘sanctifies his head’ refer back to Numbers 6:9–11 quoted in §21, so Numbers 6:9 and 6:11 are cited at those clauses. ‘Emmanuel’ is a title (Isaiah 7:14), not a quotation; no citation. The Nazirite’s unshorn head (Numbers 6:5) is Cyril’s figure, not quoted; uncited. ‘ἡ ὡς ἐν ἀρχαῖς’ rendered ‘the way given at the beginning’ (the Mosaic way of life). The Philippians quotation continues across the column break: σκύ|βαλα splits, so the English breaks at ‘I count them…’ and §23 resumes with ‘rubbish’. Cyril’s Philippians text reads ‘knowledge of Jesus Christ our Lord’ (NT: Christ Jesus); kept as Cyril gives it.

title: The law made idle; doves and lamb as signs of Christ; the Nazirite’s completion offerings
english: Cyril: …rubbish, so that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that is in the law, but the righteousness that comes through faith in Jesus Christ’ (Philippians 3:8–9)?
Palladius: I know it.

Cyril: He also rebuked others for honoring the circumcision of the law after the mystery of Christ. ‘You have been cut off from Christ,’ he says, ‘you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen from grace. But we, through faith, await the hope of righteousness’ (Galatians 5:4–5). He said too that the old commandment had been made useless, since it was not without fault, and that the other, that is, the commandment of the Gospel, had been brought in to take its place (Hebrews 7:18–19; Hebrews 8:7).
Palladius: True.

Cyril: So the riddle shows that the teaching of the law has become idle. It commands Israel, who had made the vow, to be shaved as one who had incurred defilement from a dead body, that is, as one held fast in the guilt of killing the Lord; and to sanctify to God, as it were, another head of hair after the eighth day, that is, after the resurrection: the precise and finely wrought refinement and teaching of the decrees of the Gospel. To the one who grows his hair after the eighth day the law prescribed the offering of turtledoves and doves (Numbers 6:10), setting this down too as a sign of the one who cleanses the defiled, that is, of Christ. For he is signified by both: as most sweet-voiced by the turtledove, as most gentle by the dove; whereas the law is slow of tongue (Exodus 4:10) and has no gentleness, for it punishes wrongdoers at once. A lamb is also offered together with the birds (Numbers 6:12), so that Christ may be understood through them all: through the birds as from above and from heaven, through the lamb as from below and from the earth. For the Word, who is God by nature, became flesh (John 1:14). Yet even so he was and is God. He frees us from the shadow of the law and puts into the hearts of all the knowledge of his own decrees; and he makes us truly holy, cleansing us with his own blood, according to the Scriptures (Hebrews 13:12).
Palladius: That is so.

Cyril: But if, he says, the course of the vow is brought to a good end by the one who lets his hair grow after the eighth day, let him then be made complete. And he lays down how this is to be done, saying: ‘And this is the law of the one who has vowed: on the day he completes the days of his vow, he shall present himself at the doors of the tent of witness. And he shall offer his gift to the Lord: one male lamb a year old without blemish for a whole burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish for a sin offering, and one ram without blemish for a peace offering, and a basket of unleavened loaves of fine flour, loaves mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, and their grain offering and their drink offering. And the priest shall bring them before the Lord, and shall offer his sin offering and his whole burnt offering; and he shall offer the ram as a sacrifice of peace offering to the Lord, with the basket of unleavened loaves. And the priest shall…’ (Numbers 6:13–17)
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation (σκύ|βαλα) and closes Cyril’s rhetorical question from §22, so the question mark follows the citation. Philippians 3:9: Cyril reads τὴν ἐν νόμῳ (NT: ἐκ νόμου); rendered ‘that is in the law’. Galatians 5:4–5: Cyril reads ‘Ἡμεῖς δὲ διὰ πίστεως’ (NT: ἡμεῖς γὰρ πνεύματι ἐκ πίστεως); translated as Cyril gives it; ‘you who would be justified’ renders the conative present δικαιοῦσθε. The old commandment ‘made useless … not without fault … another brought in’ is Cyril’s paraphrase of Hebrews 7:18–19 (ἀθέτησις … ἀνωφελές; ἐπεισαγωγή) and 8:7 (εἰ ἡ πρώτη ἐκείνη ἦν ἄμεμπτος), which Cyril treats as Paul’s. ‘Slow of tongue’ (βραδύγλωσσος) is the LXX word for Moses in Exodus 4:10; Cyril transfers it to the law given through Moses, so the clause is cited as a clear verbal allusion. Text ‘καὶ τοιούτου νόμου βραδυγλώσσου τε ὄντος’ is awkward (possibly οὐ τοιούτου, ‘the law not being such’); either way the sense is a contrast with Christ, rendered ‘whereas the law is slow of tongue’. ‘Turtledoves and doves after the eighth day’ refers to Numbers 6:10 (‘on the eighth day’); the lamb with the birds is Numbers 6:12. ‘Cleansing us with his own blood, according to the Scriptures’: Cyril signals Scripture without quoting; nearest wording is Hebrews 13:12 (ἵνα ἁγιάσῃ διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος τὸν λαόν), cited; compare 1 John 1:7 and Hebrews 9:14. The turtledove-melody and dove-gentleness figures are uncited (no specific verse quoted). Numbers 6:13–17 follows the LXX: σωτήριον rendered ‘peace offering’ (it also means ‘salvation offering’, a sense Cyril uses in §25); θυσία αὐτῶν rendered ‘grain offering’ as in the verse’s sense; ‘προσοίσει αὐτός’ rendered ‘he shall present himself’. The quotation breaks mid-sentence at the column end (ποιήσει ὁ | ἱερεύς).

title: Hair laid on the fire: the offerings read as stages of the holy life
english: Cyril: …offer his sacrifice and his drink offering. And the one who has vowed shall shave the head of his vow at the doors of the tent of witness, and lay the hair on the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace offering. And the priest shall take the boiled arm of the ram, and one unleavened loaf from the basket, and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the one who has vowed, after he has shaved his head; and the priest shall bring them as a wave offering before the Lord. It shall be holy to the priest, together with the breast of the wave offering and the arm of the heave offering; and after this the one who has vowed shall drink wine. This is the law of the one who vows, whoever vows his gift to the Lord for his vow, besides whatever his hand can find, according to the measure of the vow he vows, according to the law of purity’ (Numbers 6:17–21). For when the one who owes God the vow to purify himself has, as it were, thrown off the burden of the coarseness of the Mosaic history, and has freed his mind from worship in type and shadows as from a long and heavy head of hair, and has instead, like hair growing again, the truly purifying knowledge and teaching of the decrees given through Christ, he will be holy and consecrated, and acceptable besides. He would offer himself to God as a fragrant aroma, and will dedicate to him, as it were an acceptable sacrifice, the glorious and blameless excellence of his own way of life. ‘For he shall bring,’ it says, ‘his gift: a lamb a year old for a whole burnt offering, and again a ewe lamb for a sin offering, and also a ram for a peace offering, and a basket of unleavened loaves moistened with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil’ (Numbers 6:14–15). By the lamb we may fitly understand the childlikeness in Christ of the one who brings the sacrifice, and by the ram what is mature in mind and, as it were, in bearing fruit. For he says: ‘Brothers, do not be children in your minds; rather, be infants in evil, but in your minds be mature’ (1 Corinthians 14:20). Between them stands the ewe lamb, offered for sin. Through this again it is easier for us to see that even the life of those who are thoroughly purified, who live, as it were, in the simplicity and innocence understood in Christ and have been made perfect in soundness of mind, is not wholly without blame, but certainly needs cleansing. For no one will possess what is wholly beyond reproach. It is reserved for Emmanuel alone, and will remain his own, to say in truth: ‘For the ruler of this age is coming, and he will find nothing in me’ (John 14:30). So in the lamb, the ewe lamb and the ram one may see what I have said. In the unleavened loaves the sincere and pure life is signified; for the most wise Paul writes somewhere to the sanctified: ‘So clean out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened’ (1 Corinthians 5:7). And in the wafer is the savor, and as it were the sweetness, of the life of the saints. We shall offer ourselves, then: as in a lamb, because of our infancy in Christ; as in a ewe lamb, because of the weakness of our nature and how easily it is driven to wrongdoing, for the female is a type of weakness; as in a ram, mature and having reached…
translator_notes: The whole section is one Cyril turn continuing from §23. Numbers 6:17–21 follows Cyril’s LXX text: βραχίων rendered ‘arm’ (English Bibles: ‘shoulder’) because Cyril reads it in §26 as a type of strength; §26 keeps ‘arm’. ἐπίθεμα rendered ‘wave offering’ and ἀφαίρεμα ‘heave offering’, following the Hebrew sense of the verse; στηθύνιον ‘breast’. ἐπὶ τοῦ στηθυνίου rendered ‘together with the breast’. ‘Fragrant aroma’ (εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας) is standard sacrificial language (Leviticus 1:9; Ephesians 5:2); no single source, so uncited. The second Numbers quotation (6:14–15) is Cyril’s loose recall with his own connectives (‘again’, ‘also’). ‘Childlikeness in Christ’ (ἡ ἐν Χριστῷ νηπιότης) may echo 1 Corinthians 3:1 (νήπιοι ἐν Χριστῷ) but Cyril uses it in a good sense; uncited. John 14:30: Cyril reads ‘ruler of this age … will find nothing in me’ (NT: τοῦ κόσμου ἄρχων … οὐκ ἔχει οὐδέν); translated as Cyril gives it. ἀκατάσκεπτον (‘beyond scrutiny’) is an odd word here and may be a corruption of ἀκατάψεκτον (‘blameless’); the sense ‘wholly beyond reproach’ fits either. εὐπάροιστον rendered ‘how easily it is driven to’. The section breaks mid-sentence (εἰς | μέτρον ἡλικίας).

title: Justified by mercy; the vow paid, the hair burned, and Christ our forerunner
english: Cyril: …the measure of the stature that is in Christ (Ephesians 4:13); as in unleavened loaves, pure; as in wafers, sweet; yet as those who have received mercy through Christ. For we have been justified not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his great mercy (Titus 3:5). That is why the oil was rightly poured on the loaves. The priest again acts as mediator, and brings first the sin offering, then the whole burnt offering, and third, after these, the ram of the peace offering (Numbers 6:16–17). For with Christ mediating and bringing us to God the Father, we shall be accepted as we bring prayers for our own sins and ask forgiveness for our former offenses. We are also offered as whole burnt offerings in a spiritual sense, that is, entirely and completely, holy and consecrated, and we shall be dedicated to God as a fragrant aroma, not divided toward the things of the world; for the whole burnt offering was consumed entire by the fire. We shall also dedicate thank offerings for our own salvation and life, honoring God not with perishable and earthly things, but bringing him, as it were, a guest’s gift fit to be accepted: a life that is pure and unleavened, sweet and holy; for such, in some way, is the life of the saints. When the priest has brought the sacrifice according to the law, ‘Let the one who has vowed shave his head,’ it says, ‘at the doors of the tent of witness, and lay the hair on the fire’ (Numbers 6:18).
Palladius: And what do you say this means?

Cyril: The paying of the vow, and so to speak the fulfillment of what was promised. For we shall not take the manner of the shaving here to be like that of the one defiled by a dead body, who shaved off hair already most dishonored and profane. Rather, as one already made perfect in Christ, who has grown another head of hair after the eighth day, he dedicates to God, as in a type, what he promised. And the sign that God has accepted the offering is that the hair is consumed by fire; for the holy Scripture always clothes the divine nature in the form of fire. Indeed, the inspired Moses said: ‘Our God is a consuming fire’ (Deuteronomy 4:24), likening to fire, I think, the all-powerful might of the divine and pure nature. Notice how the shaving at the completion, that is, the end of all our righteousness and purification, takes place at the doors of the tent. For how could whatever purity and righteousness may come from us, on their own, bring us into the Holy of Holies, when they are not wholly free from blame and fault? ‘For no one is wholly clean from filth’ (Job 14:4). But Christ brings us in, setting us free without holding our wrongs against us, and releasing us from every sin. For he has entered as a forerunner on our behalf (Hebrews 6:20), not, surely, for himself, but for those outside the doors who have now come, in a way, to the very threshold of the holy tent, smoothing the way in for them.
Palladius: True.
Cyril: For he is said to have opened for us a new… (Hebrews 10:20)
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence (μέτρον ἡλικίας … τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ, Ephesians 4:13 wording: εἰς μέτρον ἡλικίας τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ). Titus 3:5 is quoted loosely: ‘justified’ draws on 3:7 and ‘great mercy’ (τὸ πολὺ αὐτοῦ ἔλεος) matches 1 Peter 1:3; cited at Titus 3:5. Oil poured on the loaves: Cyril plays on ἔλεος (mercy) and ἔλαιον (oil); the pun cannot be kept in English. ‘Bringing us to God’ may echo 1 Peter 3:18 (ἵνα ἡμᾶς προσαγάγῃ τῷ Θεῷ) and Christ as mediator 1 Timothy 2:5; general, uncited. ‘Not divided toward the things of the world’ may echo 1 Corinthians 7:33–34 (μεμέρισται); uncited. Thank offerings ‘for our own salvation’ play on σωτήριον (peace offering, literally ‘offering of salvation’). Numbers 6:18 is given in Cyril’s own imperative form. ‘Our God is a consuming fire’: Cyril names Moses, so Deuteronomy 4:24 is cited (LXX: κύριος ὁ θεός σου πῦρ καταναλίσκον ἐστίν; compare Deuteronomy 9:3); his wording ‘our God’ matches Hebrews 12:29. Job 14:4 LXX: τίς γὰρ καθαρὸς ἔσται ἀπὸ ῥύπου; ἀλλ᾽ οὐθείς — Cyril compresses it. Hebrews 6:20: πρόδρομος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν εἰσῆλθεν (Cyril: εἰσελήλακεν). The section ends inside πρόσφα|τον (Hebrews 10:20, ‘a new and living way’); the English stops at ‘a new…’ so that §26 resumes with ‘and living way’; Hebrews 10:20 is cited here at the break. σκηνή is ‘tent’ throughout Book 16, as in ‘tent of witness’ (σκηνὴ τοῦ μαρτυρίου).

title: The boiled arm, the bread and the wafer: Christ receives the gifts
english: Cyril: …and living way (Hebrews 10:20). After the man has come to the very doors of the holy tent and been shaved, and has burned his hair in the fire (Numbers 6:18), it says: ‘The priest shall take the boiled arm of the ram, and a loaf and a wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the one who made the vow; and taking them up again,’ it says, ‘he shall bring them as an offering before the Lord, and it shall be holy to the priest, like the breast of the portion set apart’ (Numbers 6:19–20).
Palladius: Then what would the law mean to show by this?

Cyril: In the God-inspired Scripture the arm is always understood as a type of what is strong, that is, of achievements done in strength; the unleavened bread, in turn, as a type of a holy and pure life; and the wafer, kneaded with oil and made into a flat cake, would show in itself what is gracious and sweet. One may very fittingly assign the role of the mediating priest to Emmanuel. So the one who has achieved the highest purity, and has brought a splendid offering to the all-pure God, lays upon his own hands, so to speak, the works that come from strength (clearly spiritual strength), as in the arm of the ram; a blameless life, understood as in the unleavened bread; and the sweetness and grace of a life lived in holiness, as in the wafer. These he offers up to God through Christ the mediator, who receives the gifts, as it were, from hand to hand, and honors the truly genuine worshipper with the highest honors, above all in this. That is why it says that the one who completes so holy and all-pure a vow, having laid them on his own hands, will hand them to the priest as an offering, a choice portion assigned to him, just like the breast of the ram, as the lawgiver decided. Just as we say that the arm signifies achievements that come from strength, or strength itself, so the breast of the ram signifies understanding and mind. For we have our understanding in our inward parts and in the breast. And divine Scripture often makes no distinction: sometimes it takes the head as a type of the mind, sometimes it uses the breast to indicate understanding. Holy and choice, then, and all but brought from hand to hand, and well received through him by God the Father, are the spiritual strength of those who are being made pure, and their understanding as well. For it is true to say that the saints could never succeed in doing what pleases God in any other way than through spiritual strength and a good understanding.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: He ordered the arm to be taken boiled, so as to drive away from the strength of the saints whatever is, so to speak, raw and out of keeping with what is fitting. For those dedicated to God must not be harsh, nor have a mind that is untempered; they must press on to achieve what belongs to virtue gently, tenderly and with great skill. In this way, and in no other, would the achievements of the saints be wholesome and fit food for God,…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: §25 ends 'Αὐτὸς γὰρ ἡμῖν ἐγκαινίσαι λέγεται πρόσφα[τον]' and §26 begins 'τόν τε καὶ ζῶσαν ὁδόν', so the section starts 'Cyril: …and living way', as at every continuation in Book 16. Numbers 6:18 (shaving at the door of the tent, hair put on the fire) is paraphrased, not quoted; cited as a clear reference. Numbers 6:19–20 is quoted loosely from the LXX (Cyril drops 'one unleavened loaf from the basket' and turns 'with the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the heave offering' into 'like the breast of the portion set apart'); ἐπίθεμα rendered 'offering', ἀφαίρεμα 'portion set apart'. βραχίων kept as 'arm' (English Bibles say 'shoulder') because Cyril's reading depends on the arm as the figure of strength. ἁγνεία / ἁγνίζομαι rendered 'purity' / 'being made pure' (the Nazirite consecration of Numbers 6). Final 'Εἴπερ ἔστιν ἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν' read as causal ('For it is true to say'), the usual force of εἴπερ in Cyril. Uncited possible allusions: 'Christ the mediator' (compare 1 Timothy 2:5) and 'the truly genuine worshipper' (compare John 4:23, the verse behind the work's title); both are standing Cyrilline phrases rather than clear quotations, so left uncited. The section ends mid-sentence; the clause 'τὸ ὠμὸν οὐκ ἔχοντα' falls in §27, so the English breaks after 'fit food for God,…'.

title: Nothing raw before God; vows must be kept without delay
english: Cyril: …with nothing raw or distasteful about them. You have learned, I think, that the one who lives in purity serves as saving food, food that Christ, as it were, calls his own when he says to the holy disciples: ‘I have food to eat that you do not know’ (John 4:32). Remember too that he commanded the lamb to be slaughtered as a type of Christ (Exodus 12:6), and laid down a further law, saying: ‘You shall not eat any of it raw, nor boiled in water, but only roasted with fire’ (Exodus 12:9). By ‘raw’ he means, I think, what is unacceptable and, as it were, hard to digest. So he says that the arm must be taken boiled, since what is uncooked signifies what is neither sweet nor fit to eat, and therefore unacceptable.
Palladius: How very subtle, and how true, the argument is!

Cyril: So we must pay to God what we have promised, and whatever anyone vows, let him carry it out without delay. For I would count failing to do such things promptly among the most dreadful and dangerous of faults, and so does sacred Scripture itself. If, thinking rightly, we reckon it among the most outrageous things to be convicted on a charge of lying, how would it not be utterly shameful to pledge something and promise it to God, and afterwards to prove false to that promise? So whenever anyone has vowed and then delayed, or has even shrunk back from paying altogether, the law records it against him as sin (Deuteronomy 23:21). But it releases from the charge those who have nothing at all of their own, but are yoked as by a binding necessity and act under another’s hand. It is written thus in Numbers: ‘And Moses spoke to the rulers of the tribes of the sons of Israel, saying: This is the word that the Lord has commanded. Any man who vows a vow to the Lord, or swears an oath, or binds himself with a pledge, shall not profane his word; he shall do all that comes out of his mouth. And if a woman vows a vow to the Lord, or binds herself with a pledge in her father’s house in her youth, and her father hears her vows and the pledges with which she has bound herself, and her father keeps silent, then all her vows shall stand, and all the pledges with which she has bound herself shall remain binding on her. But if her father firmly forbids it on the day he hears all her vows and her pledges with which she has bound herself, they shall not stand, and the Lord will cleanse her, because her father forbade it’ (Numbers 30:1–5). And even if, it says, the woman is lawfully married to a husband, the same law is to hold (Numbers 30:6–8). For a widow, however, and for a divorced woman, he lets the pledges stand (Numbers 30:9), and says, very rightly, that the promises must be carried out in every way and by all means. Everywhere he holds anyone who is free and outside the yoke liable to blame, if they will not choose to do what they promised; but anyone not so placed, who has no power to act and lives under others, he rightly releases. For against the masters, I mean the father and the husband, if they have agreed and, as it were, nodded assent…
translator_notes: Opens with the end of the §26 sentence ('τὸ | ὠμὸν οὐκ ἔχοντα καὶ ἀπηχθημένον'), so the section opens 'Cyril: …'. Doubtful syntax: 'Διεπύθου δέ που τὸν ἐν ἁγνείαις ἐπὶ τὴν σωτήριον τροφήν' has no expressed verb for τόν; ἐπί + accusative is read here as 'serves as' ('the one who lives in purity serves as saving food, food that Christ calls his own'), following John 4:34–36, where Christ's food is doing the Father's will and gathering the harvest; the sense, from John 4:32–34, is that a pure life is food Christ calls his own. τόν could also stand for an understood λόγον; the reading is uncertain. Exodus 12:6 cited for the command to slaughter the lamb (a clear reference, not a quotation); Exodus 12:9 quoted from the LXX. Deuteronomy 23:21 (English) = Deuteronomy 23:22 (LXX/Hebrew) is the Scripture behind 'records it against him as sin'; Ecclesiastes 5:4–5 ('do not delay to pay it') is a further possible echo of 'without delay', left uncited. Numbers 30 numbering: Cyril's quotation is LXX/Hebrew Numbers 30:2–6 = English Numbers 30:1–5; the married-woman summary is English 30:6–8 (LXX 30:7–9); widow and divorced woman English 30:9 (LXX 30:10). ὁρισμός rendered 'pledge' (a binding obligation); 'περὶ/κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς' rendered 'himself/herself' (Hebraism). καθαριεῖ kept as 'will cleanse her' (LXX for 'will forgive her'). ἐκβεβλημένη rendered 'divorced woman'. ψευδοεπείας ἁλῶναι γραφῇ is legal language (convicted on an indictment for lying). The section ends mid-sentence; the main verb ('he brings the charge of impiety') falls in §28.

title: Vows of those under authority; offerings must be freely given
english: Cyril: …to the vows of those under their hand and authority, he brings the charge of impiety if they do not choose to fulfill what was promised (Numbers 30:14–15). But when they refuse, he also rules that there must be release from sin; for offerings dedicated to God are the fruits of free choice, not of compulsion.
translator_notes: Completes the sentence begun at the end of §27 (dative 'τοῖς κυρίοις ... συνθεμένοις' governed by 'ἐπιφέρει γραφήν'), so the section opens 'Cyril: …'; rendered 'against the masters ... he brings the charge'. Numbers 30:14–15 (English; LXX 30:15–16): a husband who stays silent confirms the vows, and if he cancels them later he 'shall bear her iniquity'; cited as the provision Cyril summarizes. Ambiguity: 'Ἀποφάσκουσι δὲ καὶ τὸ ἀνεῖσθαι δεῖν ἁμαρτιῶν ἀπονέμει' – the dative plural points to the father or husband who refuses, but the release may be the woman's (compare 'the Lord will cleanse her', Numbers 30:5, 8, 12); English keeps it impersonal ('there must be release from sin'). 'Fruits of free choice, not of compulsion' may echo 2 Corinthians 9:7 or Philemon 1:14 but quotes neither; left uncited. This short section ends Book 16.
